The purpose of the rezoning is to allow the future development of approximately five to six detached single-family homes. Prepared and presented by: Allen Nicholls, Planning and Zoning Administrator ___ Application for Rezoning Case Number: RZ-09-26-01 Application Information Project Name: Bracqbien Rezoning Applicant: Karl and Gwen Bracqbien (property owner) Property Location: Portion of Tax Map 50-55 (Tax Map 50-55I) Total Parcel Acreage: 12.5 Acreage Proposed for Rezoning: 12.5 Zoning district: Agricultural (A-1) Proposed Zoning: Residential, Limited (R-1) Overview of Request The applicants propose to rezone an approximately 12.5-acre parcel on John Tucker Road from Agricultural (A-1) to Residential, Limited (R-1). The applicants’ stated intent is to subdivide the property into five or six residential lots of approximately two to 2.5 acres each and construct detached single-family homes. The proposed homes would be traditional, stick-built, single-story residences averaging approximately 1,200 square feet, with the possibility of attached one-car garages. The applicants Page 1 of 6 Return to Agenda have stated that the homes would be retained under common ownership and operated as longterm rental housing rather than sold as individual speculative homes or used as short-term rentals. The submitted conceptual plan illustrates both five-lot and six-lot development options. Under either option, three lots would be located along John Tucker Road. The remaining lots would be accessed through an existing 50-foot access easement along the eastern side of the property. No formal subdivision plat or site development plan is under review at this time. The current request is limited to a zoning map amendment. The submitted conceptual plan illustrates the applicants’ current intentions but does not establish the final lot configuration, entrance locations, drainfield locations, building locations, or development yield. Any future subdivision would be subject to the Madison County Subdivision Ordinance, Virginia Department of Health approval, Virginia Department of Transportation requirements, privateroad standards, applicable road-maintenance agreement requirements, and all other applicable regulations. The applicants’ stated intention to retain the homes as long-term rentals is also not, by itself, a restriction imposed by the requested R-1 zoning. Unless incorporated into an enforceable voluntary proffer or other legally acceptable restriction, the ownership and rental status of the future homes could change without an additional rezoning. Site and Surrounding Area The subject property is identified as Parcel X on a division survey dated June 4, 2026. The survey depicts Parcel X as containing 12.500 acres and being separated from a larger parent tract formerly identified as Tax Map 50-55. The subject property fronts John Tucker Road, identified on the survey as State Route 614 with a 40-foot right-of-way. The parcel has substantial frontage along John Tucker Road and also adjoins an existing 50-foot access easement recorded in Plat Book 41, Page 14. The property is identified by the applicants as vacant or in agricultural use and appears to consist primarily of open land with wooded areas along portions of its perimeter. The surrounding area is rural in appearance but contains an established pattern of single-family residential development. Nearby properties include agricultural parcels, individual residences, and the Sheffield Way residential subdivision. Residential, Limited (R-1) zoning and residential lots of a size generally comparable to those proposed are present in the surrounding area. The subject property is not served by public water or public sewer. Each future lot would therefore require an approved individual well and septic system, including adequate area for both a primary and reserve drainfield. The availability of suitable well and septic locations has not Page 2 of 6 Return to Agenda been established through the rezoning application and would be evaluated through the applicable Health Department and subdivision review processes. The conceptual plans show three proposed lots with access oriented toward John Tucker Road. Under the six-lot option, three additional lots would be served through the existing access easement. Under the five-lot option, two additional lots would use that access. Final entrance locations and configurations would be subject to VDOT and County approval. Procedural History & Public Notice Preliminary Development Review Committee A pre-application meeting was held at the July 7, 2026, meeting of the Preliminary Development Review Committee. Planning and Zoning Administrator Allen Nicholls recused himself from the Committee’s consideration of the case due to a close working relationship with the applicant. During this meeting, comments were made by stakeholders that included the following: VDOT: Matthew Mashhadi advised that, if the private-road entrance serves three parcels, the entrance would need to be constructed to VDOT low-volume commercial entrance standards. Final entrance design and permitting would be addressed during the subdivision and development process.. VDH: Emily Bourdon advised that the applicant would need to demonstrate adequate space for both a primary drainfield and a reserve drainfield for each proposed lot. Individual well and septic approvals would be required before development. Madison County Building Official: Jamie Wilks noted that the applicant is a County employee and stated that Mr. Wilks would personally handle the applicable official inspections and approvals to avoid the applicant’s involvement in the review of his own project. The Preliminary Development Review Committee recommended that the applicant submit a formal rezoning application for consideration by the Planning Commission. Planning Commission The rezoning application was received on August 20, 2026. First workshop: September 16, 2026. Second workshop: October 21, 2026 Advertising This public hearing was advertised in the Piedmont Journal Recorder the weeks of October 11, 2026 and October 18, 2026. Letters to adjacent and adjoining property owners were mailed October 9, 2026. Page 3 of 6 Return to Agenda Summary of Public Comment Written comment has been submitted by Mr. Troy Gooding. The letter is included in the information packet. His preference is 6 sites, but current perc tests have only shown 4 potential drain field locations so far. Whitman – asked if the applicant has considered ADUs in his development of the sites. Bracqbien – stated that the houses are intended for long term rental, and that ADUs are not part of the plan. Nicholls - clarified that the request is for rezoning, not subdivision approval, and that future development would require Health Department approval, including adequate drainfield and reserve areas, which could limit lot configuration. In response to Snyder, Nicholls confirmed that the parcel is legally recorded but awaiting a tax map number, which he agreed to pursue before action is taken. Whitman - questioned the potential for six additional ADUs under R-1 zoning. Nicholls confirmed that ADUs would be permitted by right, subject to applicable requirements, while Wright clarified that ADUs increase dwelling density, not lot count. Elliott - asked whether Bracqbien would proffer to prohibit ADUs. Bracqbien - declined, citing septic limitations and the possibility of future ADU rights under A-1 zoning. Nicholls - clarified that subdivision rights under A-1 zoning are currently exhausted, with one additional division available in 2029 and two in 2036. Carpenter - noted that rezoning would allow smaller, potentially more affordable rental homes than the four homes currently permitted under A-1. Whitman - questioned whether the potential density of 12 dwellings, including ADUs, aligns with the Comprehensive Plan. Gore - supported the rezoning based on the Plan’s housing objectives. Carpenter - cited existing development along John Tucker Road as consistent with the density of this proposal. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. SU-09-26-01) Cindy and John Decowski – Special Use Permit (Second Workshop) Cindy and John Decowski have applied for a special use permit to convert an existing singlefamily dwelling into a two-family dwelling (duplex) on property identified as Madison County Tax Map 30-78. The property is located at 27 Duet Road, contains approximately 5.032 acres, and is zoned Agricultural (A-1). A two-family dwelling (duplex) may be permitted in the Agricultural (A-1) Zoning District by special use permit pursuant to Article 14-3 of the Madison County Zoning Ordinance. Nicholls - reported no changes and noted that the proposed duplex would accommodate family needs where an ADU is not permitted. Decowski - confirmed that the proposed duplex would accommodate family members, as an ADU is not currently permitted in A-1 zoning. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. ZOA-10-26-01) Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance Amendment (First Workshop) Planning Commission Workshop Meeting Minutes – 10/21/2026 Page 2 of 5 Changes to the Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance are being considered to permit accessory dwelling units in the Conservation (C-1) and Agricultural (A-1) zoning districts. Nicholls - presented GIS data identifying approximately 891 C-1 parcels under 20 acres, 4,088 A-1 parcels under six acres, and 171 split-zoned parcels potentially affected by expanding ADU provisions, clarifying that actual eligibility would depend on existing dwellings and site conditions. He stated that The Commission was asked to consider whether to permit ADUs in either or both districts (A-1 and C-1) and whether to apply the same standards as residential (R1, R-2 and R-3) districts or apply different standards. Cowan - opposed extending ADUs to A-1 and C-1, citing concerns about increased residential density and preserving the County’s rural character and existing acreage requirements. Whitman - asked whether ADUs could be used as short-term rentals under the proposed ordinance. Nicholls - clarified that the state-mandated ADU requirements only apply to R-1, R-2 and R-3, allowing the County to establish separate standards in A-1 and C-1, should ADUs be allowed, including restrictions on short-term rentals, requirements for setbacks, etc. if they wish to do so. Carpenter – pointed out growing pains in neighboring counties and suggested that perhaps allowing ADUs in A-1 and C-1 as an SUP, might be the better way to handle the potential impact. Nicholls – asked that if an SUP is considered for ADUs in A-1 and C-1, then the Planning Commission should consider under what conditions they would approve or deny the SUP application. Nicholls – will send out a draft document to the Commissioners that extends the existing residential ADU provisions to include A-1 and C-1. Commissioners are asked to submit proposed changes specific to A-1 and C-1 districts for staff to compile and review at the next workshop. The Chairman opened the floor for general public comments. Hearing none, the floor was closed. (Case No. ZOA-05-26-01) Sign Ordinance Repeal and Replacement (Sixth Workshop) At the September 2, 2026, joint meeting of the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors, the Planning Commission tabled their efforts in modifying Article 12 of the zoning ordinance. The Board subsequently directed the Planning Commission to consider repealing the existing Article 12, and developing a replacement better suited for the County’s needs. Nicholls - reported receiving sign ordinance comments from six of eight Commissioners for review. He also noted Mr. Elliott’s preference for targeted amendments to the existing ordinance rather than a complete repeal and replacement. Comments received from the various Commissioners were read and discussed through the shared document included in the meeting packet. Language will be drafted to clarify that signs painted on buildings containing text, logos, or commercial advertising cannot be classified as artwork to circumvent sign regulations. It was agreed that language should be included stating that any future Dark Sky policies must be conformed to, in regard to illumination for signs. Wright - recommended allowing the Board of Supervisors to establish and amend policies governing election signage on County property rather than codifying specific restrictions. Members expressed support for this flexibility and discussed making such policies publicly available. The Chairman opened the floor to public comment. Hearing none, the floor was closed. For Planning Commission Meeting On: November 19, 2026 Prepared By: - Chariot Medlin Suggested Action: information only Attachments: lucky presentation for november meeting..pptx 14 Planning Commission 102 Zoning 15 Origins of Zoning in the USA • 1916 Zoning Resolution New York City • Adopted to protect residents from skyscrapers blocking light and air • Introduced setbacks, height restrictions, and separating residential, industrial and commercial uses • The blueprint for modern zoning nationwide 16 Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. • Village of Euclid adopted a zoning ordinance • Property owned by Ambler Realty was zoned to prevent industrial uses • Ambler contended that the ZO reduced the value violating their rights to liberty and property under the due process and equal protection clauses of the 14th Amendment • The Supreme Court concluded that the speculative damages claimed by Ambler Realty were insufficient to invalidate an otherwise valid exercise of the village's police power. 17 What are Police Powers • The Tenth Amendment of the Constitution states “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” • Police powers are the fundamental ability of a government to enact laws to coerce its citizenry for the public good, although the term eludes an exact definition • The states have broad authority to regulate and is limited by the state and federal constitution 18 Important Supreme Court Cases • Buchanan v. Warley (1917) – race-based zoning violates the 14th Amendment • Nollan v. California Coastal Commission (1987) – the Essential Nexus test, there must be a nexus between legitimate state interests and conditions for a permit • Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Commission (1992) – total takings test, a taking occurs when regulation denies all economically beneficial or productive use of land • Doland v. City of Tigard (1994) – conditions of a permit must be proportional to the adverse impacts of a new development • Kelo v. City of New London (2005) – a government taking of property from one owner to another in the furtherance of economic development is a permissible public use under the 5th Amendment 19 Types of Zoning • Euclidean zoning – land use by type (residential, commercial, industrial) • Flat zoning – each use is only permitted in its corresponding zone • Hierarchical zoning – less intense uses are permitted in higher intensity zones. Pyramid structure • Form Based - land development regulation that fosters predictable built results and a walkable public realm by using physical form. He also reported that traffic for the Route 17 northbound bridge project at Dragon Run has been transferred to the southbound side and that the project is moving forward, with completion expected in 2028. Back to Agenda 2 BOS Board Packet Page 4 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES October 6 , 2026 Mr. Horne also updated the Board regarding the Deltaville sidewalk project. He stated that the first portion of the project would begin at the rescue squad and extend to Green Cove Road. He stated that the original project involved a shared-use path, but the scope had been changed to a five-foot sidewalk due to citizen concerns regarding encroachment and the width of the path. He stated that the first local allocation to be billed for preliminary engineering, design, survey, environmental work, and right-of-way is $327,480, with the remaining $273,520 expected to be billed in August 2027. The Board asked whether changing the project from a shared-use path to a five-foot sidewalk would result in any savings to the County. Mr. Horne stated that he could not answer at that time but would check and report back. He also stated that there is no confirmed project completion date at this time. SCHOOLS: Dr. Tracy Seitz addressed the Board regarding two school budget supplements, FY 2027-01 and FY 2027-02. Dr. Seitz stated that both budget supplements involved carryover funds from the FY 2025-2026 budget to the FY 2026-2027 budget. Dr. Seitz stated that the first budget supplement included carryover funds for textbooks, school nutrition, small capital improvements, and the Summer Regional Governor’s School, for which Middlesex County Public Schools serves as fiscal agent. She stated that the second budget supplement included carryover for federal funds, including Title funds and IDEA funds, as well as a grant and payment from the Virginia Department of Education. Supervisor Jessie made a motion to approve School Budget Supplements FY 202701 and FY 2027-02, which was seconded by Supervisor Bill Harris. The following roll call carried the motion: Supervisor Jessie – Aye; Supervisor Williams – Aye; Supervisor Bill Harris – Aye; Supervisor Crittenden – Aye; and Chairman Don Harris – Aye. Dr. Seitz also updated the Board regarding the high school gym. She stated that the school division was waiting on the insurance adjuster and appraiser for next steps and that she had contacted VaCorp to ask that the matter be moved forward due to the gym being used by both the school division and the community. The Board also discussed the high school drainage issue. Dr. Seitz stated that Dustin Harris, the school division’s operations director, met with Mr. Gentry and Mr. Chip England, County Engineer, to review plans from the 2002 high school renovation and a subsequent athletic complex addition. She stated that staff had been unable to locate civil engineering information showing whether drainage had been rerouted. The Board discussed continuing the investigation, including the possibility of inspecting the drainage system with a camera. EDA MARKETING: Report Only. SOCIAL SERVICES: Back to Agenda 3 BOS Board Packet Page 5 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES October 6 , 2026 Report Only. CHESAPEAKE BAY PUBLIC ACCESS AUTHORITY PRESENTATION: Mr. Lewis Lawrence, with the Middle Peninsula Planning District Commission and the Middle Peninsula Chesapeake Bay Public Access Authority, addressed the Board regarding dredging and the development of a municipal dredging program. Mr. Lawrence stated that dredging is becoming a local government responsibility due to reduced federal involvement, which creates policy questions for localities regarding where to dredge, why to dredge, and how to determine what is in the public interest. Mr. Lawrence stated that dredging is an issue of greater than local concern and that jurisdictions across the Middle Peninsula are facing the same challenges. He discussed the importance of maintaining marine highways for the local economy, boating safety, the seafood industry, waterfront property values, and local tax revenue. He stated that Middlesex County has seven federal channels, the most of any locality in the Middle Peninsula, and that many shallow-water dredging projects are receiving little or no federal funding. Mr. Lawrence stated that one of the most difficult issues is not only dredging itself, but where dredged material will be placed. He explained that dredge-material placement sites and local cooperation agreements are critical and that the Corps of Engineers is moving away from recognizing certain easement placement areas. He stated that, absent a placement strategy, dredging projects may not be able to move forward or may become significantly more expensive. Mr. Lawrence discussed possible funding and organizational tools, including service districts, tax increment financing, sanitary districts, community development authorities, VRA loans, one-time grants, and public-private partnerships. He stated that service districts may provide local governments with flexibility and a predictable revenue stream for dredging needs, but each creek would need a revenue-generating strategy before moving forward. Mr. Lawrence stated that two legal documents are needed to activate participation in the municipal dredging program: an operating agreement and an operating program. He stated that the documents have been reviewed through the Virginia Port Authority and Sans Anderson and that participating jurisdictions would have a seat at the table and access to state funding. He stated that the County would need to determine whether to participate and which creeks or channels it may want included. The Board discussed staff workload and whether participation in a regional program would reduce the burden on County staff. Mr. Lawrence stated that the intent is for the Public Access Authority to serve as the agent on behalf of participating localities and to reduce the need for County staff to manage dredging projects directly, although certain federal cooperation documents may still require local government action. The Board also discussed how dredging priorities would be determined. Mr. Lawrence stated that prioritization is a local policy decision and could be based on federal channels, commercial activity, economic development, real estate value, public need, or other local considerations. He stated that public input and surveys may help identify where consistent dredging needs exist. Back to Agenda 4 BOS Board Packet Page 6 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES October 6 , 2026 DELTAVILLE COMMUNITY ASSOCIATION: Ms. Ricardi addressed the Board on behalf of the Deltaville Community Association regarding a request to waive building permit fees for renovations to the DCA pool bathrooms. He stated that the County has traditionally considered waiving building permit fees when a local nonprofit organization is completing renovations that improve community facilities and services. Ms. Ricardi stated that the Deltaville Community Association requested waiver of the building permit fees in the amount of $516 for the pool bathroom renovation project. Supervisor Williams made a motion to approve the request to waive the Deltaville Community Association pool bathroom building permit fees in the amount of $516, which was seconded by Supervisor Bill Harris. REGULAR AGENDA ITEMS VACO VOTING CREDENTIALS: Ms. Ricardi addressed the Board regarding the Virginia Association of Counties voting credentials. She stated that the Board has historically selected Supervisor Jessie to serve as the County’s voting representative for the VACo meeting. Supervisor Bill Harris made a motion to appoint Supervisor Jessie as Middlesex County’s voting representative for the VACo meeting, which was seconded by Supervisor Crittenden. The following roll call carried the motion: Supervisor Bill Harris – Aye; Supervisor Crittenden – Aye; Supervisor Jessie – Aye; Supervisor Williams – Aye; and Chairman Don Harris – Aye. CONSIDERATION OF LETTER OF SUPPORT FOR NORTHERN NECK AND MIDDLE PENINSULA REGIONAL HOUSING ASSESSMENT: Ms. Darlene Watson addressed the Board regarding the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula Regional Housing Assessment. Ms. Watson stated that she serves as the Community Network Builder for the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula through the Institute for Engagement and Negotiation at the University of Virginia. Ms. Watson stated that the proposed regional housing assessment would include all ten counties in the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula. She stated that the County was not being asked to provide funding, but was being asked to provide a letter of support and to cooperate with the data analysis, interviews, and community engagement needed for the assessment. Ms. Watson stated that the project is being funded by a $200,000 Virginia Housing grant, or approximately $20,000 per county. She stated that the assessment would include county-level, planning district-level, and full regional deliverables. She also stated that Virginia Tech would complete the data collection and Housing Forward Virginia would Back to Agenda 5 BOS Board Packet Page 7 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES October 6 , 2026 assist with the final analysis. The full process is expected to take approximately three years, with the main data portion expected to be completed within the first two years. Supervisor Crittenden made a motion to approve the letter of support for the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula Regional Housing Assessment, which was seconded by Supervisor Jessie. The following roll call carried the motion: Supervisor Crittenden – Aye; Supervisor Jessie – Aye; Supervisor Williams – Aye; Supervisor Bill Harris – Aye; and Chairman Don Harris – Aye. SURPLUS ITEMS: Ms. Ricardi addressed the Board regarding surplus property from the Sheriff’s Office. She stated that the Sheriff’s Office had turned in two vehicles, a 1999 brown Ford F350 van and a 2008 Chevrolet Suburban. She stated that the vehicles were no longer being used and were ready to be sold at auction. Staff requested that the Board declare the vehicles surplus and authorize staff to proceed with the sale. Supervisor Jessie made a motion to declare the 1999 brown Ford F350 van and 2008 Chevrolet Suburban surplus property and authorize staff to proceed with sale of the vehicles, which was seconded by Supervisor Crittenden. The County’s Comprehensive Plan designates the property as Rural Areas and Protected Lands. Sean Clendening presented the case including the location, zoning, future land use, conceptual layout, proffers, and building elevations. Mr. Hatcher asked if the adjacent parcel to the property is designated as Gateway Business. Mr. Clendening showed the future land use map showing that the adjacent areas are designated Rural Areas and Protected Lands. Brady Deal, the applicant, spoke on his company, Main Street Homes, on the land used around the area, proffers, and VDOT requirements. Mr. Hatcher asked about the housing options the development provides. Mr. Deal mentioned the lots will sell as the market dictates, but floorplans will be 2,000 square feet or more. Mr. Hatcher asked if the taper would fit inside the VDOT right-of-way. Mr. Deal said they feel comfortable with the VDOT right-of-way width, but if they need to acquire more land, they will have to do that. Mr. Hatcher asked about the left turn lane conflict with the property across the highway. Mr. Deal stated that they provide VDOT turn lane modeling and that is how VDOT reviews and approves it. Ms. Bowlin asked about the price range for the houses. Mr. Deal responded that a new construction home would not likely be less than $600,000. 7 Chair Hughes opened the public hearing. Carl Schwendeman, 1727 Theresa Lane, asked about putting in a full turn lane now rather than later. He also mentioned putting in a sidewalk or trail with buffering. Keith Buch, 2246 Branch Forest Way, stated that Main Street Homes is preferred developer and mentioned the Mill Quarter area and stated support for the project. Mark Adams, 4365 Steiger Creek Drive, asked what the buffer between the creek and the houses would be, and stated that he supports the turn lane. Seeing no one else come forward, Chair Hughes closed the public hearing. Mr. Hatcher asked for clarification on the buffer the speaker mentioned. Mr. Clendening responded that it would be 100 feet and 25 feet for structures off that. Ms. Bowlin mentioned that the subdivision to the north was an average of five acres with a two-acre minimum. Mr. Hatcher discussed the context for traffic heading west on Route 60. Vice-Chair Hall discussed the number of trucks heading down the road and stated that a turn lane would be warranted in this case. Ms. Bowlin asked about the turn lane proffer. Mr. Deal stated that there is about 30 or 40 feet of width for a taper and will have enough width for a vehicle. He stated the issue is that VDOT will require 400’ length for a full turn lane and will not give a half of a turn lane. He stated that the number of vehicles from the new lots is low compared to the church next to them, and it is unlikely VDOT will warrant a turn lane. Mr. Hatcher stated that a ten-lot private road would not be required to do a turn lane and are prevalent in Powhatan. Ms. Bowlin mentioned that most of those are on rural roads and not on Route 60. Mr. Hatcher made a motion to recommend approval of Case 26-07-REZ-C with proffered conditions. 8 . Ms. Winall seconded. Hatcher, Winall, Bowlin AYE. Hughes, Hall NAY. He showed the proposed changes as they relate to manufactured homes, solar energy facilities, high energy use facilities, off-street parking, and home-based child care. H2H has recently purchased Delta Response Team's (DRT) operation and will be taking over its services in the area. Virginia Emergency Medical Services regulations require local governing body approval for EMS agencies that maintain an office, station an ambulance for response, or operate as a Designated Emergency Response Agency (DERA) within a locality. The proposed resolution would authorize H2H to provide ALS ambulance transport services within Prince Edward County, including interfacility transports, hospital discharges, and other medically necessary patient transportation, subject to applicable Virginia Office of Emergency Medical Services licensure requirements. This authorization would not designate H2H as a primary 911 emergency response agency or assign the organization a primary emergency response district. The County's existing Designated Emergency Response Agencies and established EMS response arrangements would remain unchanged. Attachments: Hospital 2 Home Emergency Services - ALS Transport Resolution Recommendation: Staff recommends that the Board of Supervisors approve the resolution authorizing Hospital 2 Home Emergency Services to provide Non-DERA Advanced Life Support ambulance transport services within Prince Edward County, subject to applicable state licensure requirements and County agreements. The Level II Home Business will consist of cabinet and custom furniture fabrication and related accessory structures. -Brenna Menefee Special Use Permit (Special Use Permit 26-11-02): A Special Use Permit pursuant to Section 165-12B(3)(oo) of the County Code allowing 10 bedrooms for short-term rental on 57.341 acres, more or less, on certain real property zoned A-1 Agriculture, located at 1565 Seven Fountains Road (Tax Map No. 061A141H and 061A141B). The short-term rentals will consist of a primary dwelling with 6 bedrooms, an accessory dwelling with 4 bedrooms, and related accessory structures. – McKenzie Allen Zoning Text Amendment (Zoning Text Amendment 26-11-01): A Zoning Text Amendment to amend Article I, “Purpose, Title and Definitions,” Article III, “District Regulations,” Article XXI, “Decommissioning,” Article XXII, “Energy Facilities,” and Article XXIII, “Data Center Development,” of Chapter 165 of the Shenandoah County Code. The Amendment updates definitions and regulations applicable to large-scale energy facilities, data centers, and on-site power generation facilities; establishes separate special use permit requirements for on-site power generation facilities; and updates application, siting, operational, noise, screening, water-resource, environmental, monitoring, and decommissioning requirements. -Lemuel Hancock Fee Schedule Amendment (Fee Schedule Amendment Number 26-11-01): An Amendment to Chapter A170 of the Shenandoah County Code to amend Section A170-1C, which imposes building-related fees as authorized by Virginia Code Section 36-105. The Amendment would include language requiring third party review to be billed to the applicant. -Lemuel Hancock (Continued on next page) 600 North Main Street, Suite 107 | Woodstock, Virginia 22664 | 540-459-6185 https://www.shenandoahcountyva.gov/197/Planning-Commission Fee Schedule Amendment (Fee Schedule Amendment Number 26-11-02 and 26-11-03): An Amendment to Chapter A170 of the Shenandoah County Code to amend Section A170-5 in its entirety to increase or add and adopt (i) certain zoning fees as authorized by Virginia Code Section 15.2-2286(A)(6). The specific fees being added or adopted, and the amounts thereof, are as set forth below: New Proposed Fees: Special Use Permits: Data Center: $15,000; Onsite Power Generation Facility: $15,000. Third-Party Review: Applicants shall pay review costs in addition to application fees, plus any administrative fee not exceeding 5% of review costs. Payment in full is required before final approval becomes effective. -Lemuel Hancock ADJOURNMENT – BOARD OF SUPERVISORS PUBLIC COMMENT NOT PREVIOUSLY, OR TO BE, DISCUSSED AS PART OF A PUBLIC HEARING OLD BUSINESS – None NEW BUSINESS 1. December 3rd, 2026 Planning Commission Meeting ADJOURNMENT 600 North Main Street, Suite 107 | Woodstock, Virginia 22664 | 540-459-6185 https://www.shenandoahcountyva.gov/197/Planning-Commission MINUTES OF MEETING OF THE SHENANDOAH COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION October 1, 2026 A regular meeting of the Shenandoah County Planning Commission was held in the Board Meeting Room, 600 North Main Street, Woodstock, Virginia on October 1, 2026. The following members of the Planning Commission were present: Tommy Miller, Keith Stephens, Debbie Keller, James Fagan, Gary Lantz, Eunice Terndrup, and Supervisor Dennis Morris. The following members of the Board of Supervisors were present: Tim Taylor, David Ferguson, Mark Dotson, Steve Baker and Kyle Gutshall. Others present included Director of Community Development Lemuel Hancock, Zoning Administrator Brenna Menefee, County Planners McKenzie Allen and Jack Hurst, and Permit Technician, Summer Andes. An invocation was given, followed by the Pledge of Allegiance. Keith Stephens made a Motion, seconded by James Fagan, to approve the agenda, with an amendment to change Section 2, under Public Hearings; the 4th to last word should read yard instead of years. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. James Fagan made a Motion, seconded by Eunice Terndrup to approve August 27, 2026 minutes. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. Debbie Keller made a Motion, seconded by Eunice Terndrup to amend the September 3, 2026 minutes due to typographical errors discussed with staff. A vote of 7-0 approved the Motion as follows: Ayes: Miller, Stephens, Keller, Fagan, Lantz, Terndrup and Supervisor Morris. Supervisor Tim Taylor called the Board of Supervisors to order. REPORTS An update was given by Tumbling Run about the 2026 season. Two large rodeos were held; one in June, which sold out, and one in September, which sold about 1,200 tickets. Another rodeo was held for charity in July. 2027 Tumbling Run is planning two large rodeos and two for charity. Amy Dill and Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation about Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) for Fiscal Year 2028 – 2032. In September a Capital Planning Work Session was held, and some survey results were received from Planning Commission. They asked, moving forward into November, for a vote from PC to move forward to the Board of Supervisors for their Work Retreat and discussing the annual budget. Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation on ordinance reviews and updates: Decommissioning, Energy and Data Centers. He stated that currently, if an application is received, the standard fee level of $500 is used. He proposed to increase the application fees, for Data Center and Onsite Power Generation Facilities, at the November PC meeting. Any Third-Party review would be passed on to the applicant, and that would be included in the Building Code and Zoning Code fee schedules. Lemuel Hancock asked for a PC recommendation to have a public hearing about this. Keith Stephens asked if the fees being addressed were enough to cover the reviews for Data Centers and Onsite Power Generation Facilities. Lemuel Hancock answered that $5,000 was the previous high, and when staff checked with other communities, they found that they had Data Center specific fees, and they were five to six times higher. He felt the $5,000 would work for our area but stressed that currently the fee is only $500. Page 1 The PC gave an “All in Favor” vote to update the fee schedule for Data Centers and Onsite Power Generation Facilities and present at the November PC meeting. PUBLIC HEARINGS 1. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-01. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to revise the definition of “Garages, Public” to add that certain uses including, but not necessarily limited to, renting, selling, or storing motor vehicles, are “permitted as an accessory use only to a permitted public garage”. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that the primary use of the business would have to be servicing, repairing or equipping motor vehicles. Then, as an accessory use, they could also rent, sell or store motor vehicles. 2. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-02. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to make certain amendments to the definition of “Inoperative Motor Vehicles”, which amendments include, but are not necessarily limited to, (i) clarifying that trailers or semi-trailers can be Inoperable Motor Vehicles, and (ii) providing that vehicles that do not have valid license plates and valid inspection decals, unless exempt, are Inoperable Motor Vehicles, and (iii) requiring that Inoperable Motor Vehicles shall not be parked or stored in the required front yard at any time. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. James Fagan stated this was more of a prohibited use, rather than a definition. Tommy Miller agreed that this was not a definition. Keith Stephens stated that farmers use trailers for farming, and they may not have tags on them. Brenna Menefee stated that they would not be able to park them in the front yard, but if they were Farm Use, they would have proper things from DMV that would exempt them. Dennis Morris asked for clarification as to what exactly is allowed. He stated that Farm Use Vehicles can sometimes sit in the yard years. Brenna Menefee explained that this amendment would help to make things clearer. She told PC that staff pursues many issues where they end up in court. She stated that many times the complainant has an issue with the vehicles being parked near the road/front yard; telling the violator that they cannot have more than five vehicles, because that makes them a Vehicle Graveyard, does not satisfy that complainant, because many times there are not more than five vehicles, but they are by the road. Mark Dotson stated that a farmer can use a semi-trailer box as storage, with or without wheels, without Farm Use tags. Brenna Menefee explained that storage trailers on the ground are not considered vehicles, and currently code does not allow those containers to be set just anywhere. They have been allowed as accessory use, if they are screened appropriately and on ag land or industrial land; not subdivisions. Mark Dotson stated that after reading through our Zoning Code, he saw that we are missing several aspects of State Code that we reference with screening or shield of view. He explained that we do not want to have a negative impact on individuals that have valid uses for trailers, semi-trailers or vehicles that are currently being used. Brenna Menefee explained that she liked the verbiage of trailer and semi-trailer, because she is currently working on a violation with a right of way that is being blocked by a tractor trailer. People are having to drive around it just to get to their property. She stated that she cannot make the owner move the trailer, Page 2 but she is unwilling to drop the violation until it is moved, but she is unsure that a judge would agree with her, because the current definition does not state that the trailer cannot be there. John Price spoke against the proposed ZTA. He explained that sometimes people may not be able to fix a vehicle right away, but they do not have a place to store the vehicle while it is not operable. He felt that if the VDOT right of way is enforced, no other ordinance is needed. Josh Stevens stated that State Code pretty much says what we should do. He was concerned with the wording; it should be the same as what is used by the State. He explained that more specifics need to be given with how the code reads. He asked that three things be looked at: • • • Look at the word “and”, and how it relates to the existing State Statute Clarify, particularly with trailers that already have running gear removed, that are being used as stationary storage; does that automatically make that an inoperable vehicle Address vehicles and trailers that are truly exempt from state inspection 3. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-03. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to create a new definition for “Dwelling, Accessory Detached” that will replace the existing definition of “Dwelling, Accessory”. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that currently, in all zoning districts, a primary and an accessory dwelling are allowed. This would still allow that, but it must remain under the same ownership. 4. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-04. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-4 of the County Code to create a new definition for “Dwelling, Accessory Attached”, which definition will also contain certain requirements and regulations that pertain to Accessory Attached Dwellings. Brenna Menefee gave a presentation. She explained that currently, in all zoning districts, a primary and an accessory dwelling are allowed. This would still allow that, but it must remain under the same ownership. 5. Zoning Text Amendment 26-10-05. A Zoning Ordinance Text Amendment to amend Section 165-106 to revise certain standards and adopt new standards pertaining to the process for enforcement and revocation of special use permits. Lemuel Hancock gave a presentation. He explained that this would give a clear process of what would happen if a special use permit was violated. • Two or more violations in an 18-month period: The applicant or violator would receive a notice from the Zoning Administrator. After two of those are sent, then there will be a PC review, and possibly Board of Supervisor review John Price spoke against the ZTA proposal. He asked for more specifics on what would need to happen to make a violator more accountable. He stated that fees may not stop violators. Mr. Taylor adjourned the Board of Supervisors. Page 3 PUBLIC COMMENT NOT PREVIOUSLY, OR TO BE, DISCUSSED AS PART OF A PUBLIC HEARING Jess Estienne presented a petition she started against Special Use Permits in Fort Valley. She was concerned with light and noise pollution, wildlife safety, limited resources for rescue, traffic, roads and the historical value of the valley. OLD BUSINESS 1. Special Use Permit 26-09-01: A Special Use Permit pursuant to Section 165-11B(3)(t) of the County Code allowing a rural resort on 230.795 acres, more or less, on certain real property zoned C-1 Conservation, located at Narrow Path, Fort Valley (Tax Map No. 084A003, 072A002A, 072A002B, 07203003, 072A003B, 07203004, 07203001, 072A003A, 072A004A, 07SA004B, 07205003, 07205004, 072A018A, 072A018B, 072A020). The rural resort will consist of a retreat center and related accessory structures. Brenna Menefee gave a brief recap of the presentation, given September 3, for the proposed SUP. She explained that the applicant was offering a few additional conditions as follows: • • • • Limiting the number of events Maximum number of attendees Removing portable bathroom facilities from the property Event related lighting and amplified music to end at 10PM Lemuel Hancock stated that as of 3PM today, VDOT had replied that required site distance for the location was still not met. Kristie Rodriguez, applicant for the proposed SUP, spoke about the additional conditions that were being offered. James Fagan made the comment that the PC must make a motion tonight based on what is there now and the current information; not on what can be done or will be done. James Fagan also stated that the VDOT requirements are still not satisfied. Kristie Rodriguez said they would be willing to remove the existing sign. The applicant asked if the SUP could be tabled until the requirements were satisfied and then revisit to decide or make the SUP approval contingent on the requirements being met; giving the applicant time to finish the VDOT requirements. James Fagan said PC could not table the SUP. Tommy Miller said he did not think PC could make a decision with contingencies. Kristie Rodriguez then asked if she could table the SUP proposal until the VDOT work is done. Lemuel Hancock explained that without the applicant asking staff or putting it in writing to them, PC must make a decision. Page 4 NEW BUSINESS Keith Stephens recused himself from the vote for SUP 26-09-01 1. Gary Lantz made a Motion, seconded by Eunice Terndrup, to deny the Special Use Permit 26-09-01: A Special Use Permit pursuant to Section 165-11B(3)(t) of the County Code allowing a rural resort on 230.795 acres, more or less, on certain real property zoned C-1 Conservation, located at Narrow Path, Fort Valley (Tax Map No. 084A003, 072A002A, 072A002B, 07203003, 072A003B, 07203004, 07203001, 072A003A, 072A004A, 07SA004B, 07205003, 07205004, 072A018A, 072A018B, 072A020). text: TOWN OF BEDFORD PLANNING COMMISSION AGENDA THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 2026 2ND FLOOR COUNCIL CHAMBERS, TOWN MUNICIPAL BUILDING CALL TO ORDER DETERMINATION OF MEMBERS PRESENT AND EXISTENCE OF QUORUM REMARKS BY CHAIRMAN AND MEMBERS APPROVAL OF MINUTES: ▪ Approval of Minutes – October 1, 2026 STAFF AND COMMITTEE REPORTS UNFINISHED BUSINESS ▪ Initiation of Land Development Regulation Amendments o Subdivision Ordinance o Floodplain Ordinance – Zoning NEW BUSINESS ▪ Sign Modification – Bedford Residences LLC - Spring Oak at Bedford – The Elks Home PUBLIC COMMENTS ADJOURNMENT The next regular meeting will be Thursday, December 3, 2026, at 5:30 pm The Town will strive to provide reasonable accommodations and services for persons who require special assistance to participate in this public involvement opportunity. Contact (540) 587-6001 for more information. MinutesoftheTownofBedford PLANNING COMMISSION The regular meeting of the Planning Commission was held on Thursday, October 1, 2026, in the Town Municipal Building Council Hall. Planning Commission members present: Jason Horne, Chairman; Brock Malcolm, Vice Chair; Darryl Updike, Town Council Representative; Cynthia Gunnoe; and Philip Thompson Planning Commission member absent: Georgiann Watts and one vacancy Town Staff present: Mary Zirkle, Director of Planning and Community Development; and Cathy Johnson, Clerk of the Commission CALL TO ORDER: The Chair called the meeting to order at 5:30 pm. DETERMINATION OF QUORUM: There was a quorum to conduct business with five members present, one absent, and one vacancy. REMARKS BY CHAIRMAN & MEMBERS: Mr. Thompson reserved his time until after the subdivision ordinance review because he had questions for staff. APPROVAL OF MINUTES: Mr. Malcolm made a motion to approve the minutes, which was seconded by Mr. Updike. With six members voting aye, the September 3, 2026, minutes were approved as presented. PUBLIC HEARING: The Chair announced that the public hearing scheduled for this meeting regarding a proposed multifamily/townhouse development located off Jeter Street has been postponed at the developer’s request earlier in the day. The developer is tentatively planning a community meeting on October 20, 2026 at 6:00 pm at his office located at 101 North Bridge Street (the former Wells Fargo building). When asked by Ms. Gunnoe if the developer is planning to change his proposal, the Chair understands the developer intends to modify his proposal after receiving feedback from the community. Ms. Zirkle indicated that only a brief email was received requesting postponement; no specifics about changes to the proposal were provided at this time. Mr. Horne read the email. 10/1/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 1 of 4 The citizens present for the public hearing asked how they will be notified of the community meeting on October 20. In addition to staff, the Chair stated they will have to contact the developer. After asking staff if it is public record, Mr. Updike gave the applicant’s phone number and encouraged residents to call him directly with questions or to confirm the details. The Chair stated that the public hearing is expected to be rescheduled on November 5th provided the developer meets the required two-week public notice deadline. Mrs. Shauna Boggus asked will the public hearing follow the same notification process as before. Staff stated that the same process will apply consistent with standard notification procedures. STAFF AND COMMITTEE REPORTS: Ms. Zirkle confirmed that the concern regarding the unsafe sidewalk at the intersection of Quarles and Madison has been passed on to the appropriate department. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: Ms. Zirkle presented revised updates to the subdivision ordinance that were items of most interest. The updates focused on road design standards, pavement widths, on-street parking provisions, multi-entrance requirements, and off-site drain field prohibitions. The Commissioners discussed whether to permit on-street parking in new subdivisions. Ms. Zirkle confirmed through a recent VDOT meeting that the minimum pavement width is 30 feet and should replace the previously referenced 28 feet throughout the ordinance. Mr. Horne recommended a traversable pavement width of 36 feet face-of-curb, non-mountable curbing to still allow accessibility at driveways, and adequately accommodates on-street parking and emergency vehicle access. Ms. Zirkle researched the multi-entrance requirements on page 21, but she could not find the required text from other jurisdictions. The ordinance was updated to reflect minimum pavement widths consistent with VDOT requirements on pages 20-21. The Commission wanted to add new language requiring that subdivisions adjoining two or more streets provide entrances on at least two streets where possible, while discouraging through traffic. The text provided was copied from the multi-family section requiring connection at existing streets. Commissioners agreed that language was acceptable on page 18. Mr. Malcolm discussed the prohibition of off-site drain fields for newly created lots in town. Mr. Thompson stated the provision applies to the creation of new lots intended for development, not boundary line adjustments. Placement of this prohibition within the ordinance was debated, with staff noting it is captured in design standards but not as a required statement on the final plat. The Commissioners asked why does the ordinance include a provision allowing the Zoning Administrator to waive preliminary plan requirements if they are never waived. Ms. Zirkle answered the Town Attorney inserted permissive language from the Virginia State Code but she will review the source for clarification. Next, Ms. Zirkle provided a brief update on the status of the floodplain ordinance update, which is still in progress. The Commissioners discussed whether to hold separate public hearings for the subdivision 10/1/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 2 of 4 and floodplain ordinances or to combine them into a single advertised hearing with two separate actions. Ms. Zirkle stated either approach is feasible and by combining the hearings would reduce advertising costs. The Commissioners suggested if the floodplain ordinance is not ready, they could proceed with the subdivision ordinance public hearing. A combined public hearing was tentatively targeted for December. NEW BUSINESS: Mr. Thompson expressed concern that they frequently receive application materials too late to conduct thorough reviews, and that applications often lack sufficient detail to support informed decision-making. He offered suggestions to staff about improving the land use application submittal process for allowing adequate time for review. Ms. Zirkle stated that the timeline is driven primarily by the newspaper publication deadline, which requires ads to run two Wednesdays before the meeting. Mr. Thompson expressed interest in requiring additional details such as renderings, unit sizes, price points, traffic data. Mr. Malcolm agreed that applications have limited information. Ms. Gunnoe acknowledged there’s a balance between requiring enough information for decision-making and agreed with the suggestions. Mr. Thompson discussed the potential value of formalizing or strongly encouraging community meetings for larger or controversial development proposals. He stated these meetings allow residents to ask questions directly of the applicant, help applicants understand community concerns in advance of the public hearing, and can result in plan modifications that reduce conflict at the formal hearing. Ms. Zirkle stated although they are not currently required, she had strongly encouraged applicants applying controversial projects to talk to the affected landowners. Mr. Thompson suggested that an open house format should be hosted by Town staff at a public facility that can hold meetings, but did not want to create more work for staff. Ms. Gunnoe asked can the Planning Commission require community meetings and would changes to the application process require Council approval. Ms. Zirkle stated formalizing community meetings would likely require a policy or ordinance change approved by Council. She stated any changes to the timeline may be handled at the staff level, but changes to the information required on the application form which are tied to the zoning ordinance would likely require Council approval. Mr. Thompson asked does the Town have a threshold for requiring traffic impact studies as part of the application process. Ms. Zirkle stated no formal threshold currently exists. Mr. Thompson suggested establishing a threshold, potentially at 75 or more units, that would trigger a required traffic study with the application. He reasoned having traffic studies was a way to reduce community debate over traffic impacts at the public hearing. Ms. Zirkle stated that ideally large developments are reviewed by Michael Johnson with Hurt & Proffitt, the independent engineer consultant for the Town and he provides feedback. Mr. Updike asked what are the next steps on process reform and suggested waiting until January after new Council members are seated. Ms. Zirkle will review the current application process and explore options for extending the application timeline, increasing information requirements, and the possibility of formalizing community meeting requirements and traffic study thresholds. 10/1/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 3 of 4 Before adjourning, Mr. Malcolm announced that he will not be at the meeting in November due to training at DEQ headquarters in Richmond. ADJOURNMENT: There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 6:53 p.m. The next regular scheduled meeting will be on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 5:30 p.m. Respectfully submitted, Cathy Johnson, Clerk of the Commission Approved on November 5, 2026 Jason Horne, Chairman Footnote: An AI-generated summary was used to assist with meeting notes. 10/1/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 4 of 4 DRAFT – November 5, 2026 (October 1, 2026, September 3, 2026) For Planning Commission Review BEDFORD TOWN CODE PART III – LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS Article I. – Authority and Enactment. No change. Sec. 201. – Purpose. No change. Sec. 202. – Nonexclusionary Intent. No change. Sec. 203. – Covenants and restrictions. These regulations bear no relation to any private easement, covenant, agreement, or restriction. No public official is responsible for the enforcement of any private easement, covenant, agreement, or restriction. The Town will enforce only the provisions of these regulations. Notwithstanding this, the Council reserves the right, but not the responsibility, in its discretion, to deny a rezoning or conditional use permit application on the basis of nonconformity with private land restrictions. For purposes of this Land Development Ordinance, the following routes are identified as arterial roads: U.S. Highway 460, Route 221, and Route 43.  Easement. No change. Article X. – Administrative Procedures. Sec. 1001. – Zoning Administrator. The zoning administrator shall be the director of planning and community development or other official designated by the town managerdesignated by the town council. 1001.01. Powers and duties of the zoning administrator. The zoning administrator is authorized and empowered on behalf of and in the name of the council to administer and enforce the provisions set forth herein to include receiving applications, inspecting premises, and issuing zoning permits for uses and structures which are in conformance with the provisions of this Land Development Ordinance. The zoning administrator shall have all necessary authority on behalf of the council to administer and enforce this Land Development Ordinance, including the ordering in writing of the remedying of any condition found in violation of this Land Development Ordinance, and the bringing of legal action, including injunction, abatement, or other appropriate action or proceeding, to ensure compliance with this Land Development Ordinance. The zoning administrator does not have the authority to take final action on applications or matters involving variances on which final action is reserved for the board of zoning appeals, nor on conditional uses on which final action is reserved to the town council. In addition, the zoning administrator may, in specific cases, make findings of fact and, with the concurrence of the town attorney, conclusions of law regarding determinations of rights accruing under Code of Virginia, § 15.2-2307 or § 15.2-2311(C). Any zoning violation notice or other written order of the zoning administrator shall include a statement informing the recipient that he may have a right to appeal the notice of a zoning violation or a written order within 30 days in accordance with this Land Development Ordinance, and that the decision shall be final and unappealable if not appealed within 30 days. The zoning violation or written order shall include the applicable appeal fee and a reference to where additional information may be obtained regarding the filing of an appeal. The appeal period shall not commence until the statement is given and the written or is sent by registered or certified mail to, or pasted at, the last known address or usual place of abode of the property owner or its registered agent, if any. There shall be a rebuttable presumption that the property owner's last known address is that shown on the current real estate tax assessment records, or the address of a registered agent that is shown in the records of the clerk of the state corporation commission. 1001.02. RECONVENE IN OPEN SESSION: ACTION FOLLOWING CLOSED MEETING: ADJOURNMENT: 2 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 1 of 5 TOWN OF BOWLING GREEN TOWN COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES Thursday, October 01, 2026 6:00 PM PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE:  Mayor Tina Gambill called the Town Council Meeting to order at 6:02 PM and led the Pledge of Allegiance. Councilmembers Present: Mayor Tina Gambill, Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle, Councilmember Jean Davis, Councilmember John Chinault, Councilmember David Storke, Councilmember Randy Hageman, Councilmember Jeff Voit Councilmembers Absent: Councilmember Dan Webb Staff Members Present: John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager/Clerk; Jeff Gore, Town Attorney; Justin Cecil, Bowling Green Police Chief; Vianne Baylor, Deputy Town Treasurer; Perry Hickman, Capital Projects & Grants Manager/Assistant Town Manager; Jeffrey Smith, Administrative Assistant/Deputy Clerk. Darla Odom, Deputy Zoning Administrator, participated remotely to discuss potentials for the location of retail cannabis facilities and their regulation under the Town’s zoning ordinance CALL TO ORDER AND ESTABLISHMENT OF QUORUM:  Six Councilmembers were present, Councilmember Dan Webb was absent, and a quorum was established. CONSENT AGENDA: 1. Minutes- September 3, 2026  Councilmember Jean Davis identified a correction under Member Comments. Councilmember Jeff Voit moved to approve the September 3, 2026, minutes as corrected. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by right-hand raise, with six members voting and one absent.  Councilmember David Storke mooved to add Item 13, Proposal for Services, to the agenda. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by right-hand raise, with six members voting and one absent. PUBLIC COMMENTS: 3 MINUTES PER INDIVIDUAL  None. MEMBER COMMENTS:  Councilmember Jeff Voit reported that the Town’s Clean Sweep event had lower participation than previous events but good walk-in attendance and positive feedback. He encouraged attendance at the October 17 Harvest Festival, the Music on the Green concert the preceding evening, and the upcoming Pirate Festival in Port Royal. 3 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 2 of 5 STAFF REPORTS & PRESENTATIONS: 2. Bowling Green Police Department Report, Chief Justin Cecil  Town Council received the Bowling Green Police Department report. Chief Justin Cecil advised that Harvest Festival preparations were proceeding smoothly. Mayor Tina Gambill thanked the department for its work to keep attendees safe. 3. Utilities Report, Inboden Environmental Services  Mark Inboden presented the utilities report. Monthly water production totaled approximately 4.3 million gallons, averaging approximately 141,000 gallons per day. Wastewater flow totaled approximately 4.12 million gallons, averaging approximately 133,000 gallons per day. Effluent monitoring results were within permit limits, and no operational issues were reported. 4. Public Works Department Monthly Report, Shawn Fortune, DPW  Town Council received the Public Works Department monthly report. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino advised that Public Works Director Shawn Fortune was absent due to illness and offered to address questions. No questions were presented. 5. Finance Director/Treasurer’s Report, Vianne Baylor, Deputy Town Treasurer  Vianne Baylor presented the finance report. Council discussed unpaid utility balances associated with apparently vacant residences and whether the $250 utility deposit adequately covered those balances. Staff was asked to review the deposit amount and outstanding balances for further consideration. 6. Capital Improvement Projects Presentation, Perry Hickman, Capital Projects & Grants Manager  Perry Hickman reviewed the well-replacement and Gross Alpha treatment project, estimated at approximately $8.2 million with approximately $59,000 in annual operating and maintenance costs. Approximately $6.2 million has been allocated through the Virginia General Assembly, with the balance anticipated through EPA funding coordinated by the Virginia Department of Health (VDH). He reported that the memorandum of agreement (with who? )had been signed September 3 and that Stantec’s engineering proposal and test-well specifications had been submitted to VDH. He also reviewed the approximately $1.1 million waterline replacement project associated with Congressman Vindman’s community project funding request, including approximately $746,000 in anticipated federal funds and a $358,962 Town match whose funding source remained to be determined. The project would serve portions of Main Street, Chase Street, and North Main Street near government facilities. The containerized sludge-dewatering equipment at the wastewater treatment plant was installed on September 24 and is operating successfully. Virginia Rural Water Association camera inspections were scheduled for October 8 to help identify inflow and infiltration in select sewer collection lines, with targeted smoke testing of lines also under consideration. Recent Main Street water-main repairs for two breaks cost approximately $29,000 and $18,200, and Council discussed the deteriorated pipe condition and need for additional replacement. Mr. Hickman also reported receipt of a $5,000 Dominion Energy grant for the BGVA Main Street mural and the anticipated transfer of those funds to BGVA Main Street. No motion concerning the mural funds was made. Town Manager’s Report, John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager  Interim Town Manager John Anzivino reported on staff meetings, current projects, Harvest Festival preparations, a fiscal-impact analysis for a proposed subdivision in the Route 301 corridor project, anticipated zoning updates, and FY2026 audit preparations. He noted the need to complete financial reconciliations, develop cash-flow and capital-project funding plans, and coordinate a CivicPlus website update. He also presented a Virginia Foundation for Healthy Youth grant opportunity for playground matting, with awards up to $100,000, no local match, and reimbursement of eligible expenditures. The application deadline was October 28, and funds would need to be expended by July 15, 2027. Staff would determine the matting cost and provide a subsequent update. Councilmember Randy Hageman reported potential REC volunteer assistance for the playground installation, and staff emphasized volunteer registration. 4 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 3 of 5  Councilmember Randy Hageman moved to authorize staff to pursue grant funding for playground matting. The motion was seconded by Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: 7. Proposed Replacement of Article 4.10 — Parking Regulations  Council reviewed the proposed ordinance and discussed discrepancies between the summary and ordinance concerning large commercial vehicles, school buses, and recreational vehicles. Town Attorney Jeff Gore explained that the overnight parking provision addressed street parking and that the summary appeared to retain language from an earlier draft. Council also discussed fire-lane markings and the previously identified Lakewood Road correction. Staff reported receipt of VDOT comments concerning golf carts and was asked to follow up on fire-lane issues with VDOT and the fire department.  Councilmember David Storke moved to approve the parking ordinance as amended. The motion was seconded by Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. NEW BUSINESS: 8. Referral of Cannabis Regulations to the Planning Commission  Deputy Zoning Administrator Darla Odom presented the proposed approach to cannabis-related zoning regulations. She described the state licensing framework and the need to prepare local regulations addressing definitions, zoning districts, approval requirements, separation distances, hours, signage, odor control, security, parking, and enclosed operations. Council discussed available local authority, potential tax provisions, and consideration of practices in other jurisdictions. Council encouraged timely preparation of appropriate regulations without unnecessary complexity.  Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle moved that Town Council initiate a zoning text amendment to regulate cannabis businesses and refer the matter to the Planning Commission for consideration and a public hearing at its November 2026 meeting, with the Commission’s recommendation returned to Town Council. The motion was seconded by Councilmember David Storke and carried unanimously by roll-call vote, with six affirmative votes and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 9. Caroline Historical Society Request for Courthouse Lane Building for Storage Assistance  Caroline Historical Society President Kathy McVey requested assistance with storage, including possible donation or lease of the Town-owned Courthouse Lane building with utility costs also donated by the Town. She explained that the Society currently paid $130.50 monthly for storage and a new structure, as proposed, would also welcome space for art shows and sales. Council discussed reported the structures mold and moisture issues, possible remediation costs, liability, the original property transfer, and potential future Town staffing and records-storage needs. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino recommended assessing the building’s condition, potential uses, and improvement costs before deciding its disposition. A limited storage lease and placement of a separate storage building on Town property were discussed as possible alternatives. Council requested further investigation, including review of available inspection and repair information, before responding. No donation or lease was approved. 10. Request to Waive Town Hall Rental Fees for Bowling Green Fire Department Event  Council considered a request to waive Town Hall rental fees for the Bowling Green Fire Department’s October 3 fundraising dinner, with setup October 2. The event was expected to draw approximately 300 attendees. The fee waiver was presented as approximately $1,300. Council requested documentation of the department’s nonprofit status for Town records.  Councilmember David Storke moved to waive the rental fee. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried by roll-call vote with five affirmative votes, Councilmember Jeff Voit abstaining, and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 5 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 4 of 5 INFORMATIONAL ITEMS: 11. DOJ Web Access Ruling: WCAG 2.1 AA Requirements  Administrative Assistant/Deputy Clerk Jeffrey Smith provided an update on website accessibility planning and reported an April 26, 2028, compliance deadline. He noted that 374 of the 375 PDFs reviewed in the Town’s website compliance report had accessibility issues and were out of compliance with federal requirements. Staff was continuing to evaluate compliance options, including CivicPlus DocAccess, for which the first-year quote was $4,297. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino advised that associated costs should be considered in the FY2028 budget. Further information would be provided during the upcoming budget cycle. No action was requested or taken. PUBLIC COMMENTS: 3 MINUTES PER INDIVIDUAL  Mayor Tina Gambill did not reopen public comment because no members of the public remained to speak. MEMBER COMMENTS:  Vice-Mayor Valarie Coyle raised concerns about the possible removal of the UPS drop box and uncertainty regarding local package drop-off options. Staff agreed to investigate and provide clarification for residents.  Councilmember David Storke emphasized maintaining momentum in the Town’s intergovernmental support agreement with Fort A.P. Hill and exploring increased project limits and administrative revenue. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino reported that staff remained engaged with Fort A.P. Hill and would follow up on opportunities to expand the program. Mayor Tina Gambill recognized the partnership’s accomplishments and national award nomination.  Councilmember Randy Hageman welcomed Interim Town Manager John Anzivino and asked about FOIA and conflict-of-interest training. Mayor Tina Gambill suggested coordinated attendance at the January Virginia Municipal League newly elected officials conference. Town Attorney Jeff Gore discussed available training resources. Councilmember Randy Hageman also requested review of vehicle-repair activities, outdoor conditions, and compliance with prior approvals at the North Main Street automobile dealership.  Mayor Tina Gambill raised business concerns about the fats, oils, and grease program. Councilmember Randy Hageman relayed information from Mark Inboden concerning possible indoor grease traps and accommodations for existing businesses, with inspections and some improvements still anticipated. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino explained the program’s connection to wastewater permitting requirements. No ordinance amendment or exemption was adopted. 13. Proposal for Services  Councilmember David Storke presented a proposal from former Town Manager India Adams-Jacobs for possible transition and consulting services. Council discussed the scope, potential limitations associated with her employment elsewhere, and assistance with recruitment of a permanent Town Manager. Interim Town Manager John Anzivino recommended expanding the vacancy advertisement beyond the existing outlets to professional associations and recruitment sites in Virginia and neighboring states before deciding whether to engage an executive-search firm. Staff was directed to share the existing advertisement and broaden recruitment efforts. No consulting agreement or recruitment-firm engagement was approved. ADJOURNMENT: 12. Joint Town Council-Planning Commission Meeting and Public Hearing- October 22, 2026  Councilmember Jeff Voit motioned to recess the meeting until October 22, 2026, at 6:00 PM at Town Hall for the joint Town Council-Planning Commission meeting and public hearing. The motion was seconded by Councilmember Randy Hageman and carried unanimously by voice vote, with six members present and Councilmember Dan Webb absent. 6 Town Council Meeting October 01, 2026 Minutes Page 5 of 5 Attest: Mayor: ___ Tina Gambill Clerk: ___ John Anzivino, Interim Town Manager/Clerk Attachments Referenced During Meeting: 7 Town Council Memorandum TO: FROM: SUBJECT: DATE: The Honorable Mayor and Town Council Chief J.O.Cecil Bowling Green Police Dept.
