Mr. Hankins stated that the Wythe County Planning Commission will conduct a public hearing Monday, October 26, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. to receive public comments on the proposed Land Use Classification Ordinance of Wythe County, Virginia. The hearing will be conducted in the auditorium of George Wythe High School, 1 Maroon Way, Wytheville, VA. Citizens will be heard in the order they are received. Due to anticipated number of speakers, the citizens speaking time will be limited to three (3) minutes per person. Advanced registration is available online until noon on the day of the hearing at www.wytheco.org/zoning and in person from 5:30 p.m. until hearing time. Alternatively, written comments for the record may be received via electronic mail to Lisa Shelton, County Planner, at ldshelton@wytheco.org or by mail at 290 South Sixth Street, Suite 350, Wytheville, VA 24382. This hearing is held in compliance with Section 15.2-2204 of the Code of Virginia. The proposed ordinance and zoning map may be viewed online at www.wytheco.ord/zoning or at Wythe County Administrator’s Office, 290 South Sixth Street, Suite 350, Wytheville, VA. By Order of the Wythe County Planning Commission, David P. Midkiff, Chair. Mr. Hankins started calling the speakers up in the order they were received. Bobbi Dillow-Walsh – “I’m Bobbi Dillow-Walsh. I am a lifetime resident of Wythe and Bland County. I've lived here in Wytheville, the town, for the past 15 years. I own two properties here in the town. I also serve as an HOA president for Green for the townhouses located behind Church Street, right in the historic district. So, I've owned October 26, 2026 Public Hearing Unapproved Minutes that property and have my mother living there now. So, I wanted to come and speak tonight. I have 25 years in power systems. First with, I recognize Dave from the years at ABB, Hitachi Energy. I've worked with Schneider Electric, the world's most sustainable company, and a publicly traded utility. And now with Siemens, and my role now within Siemens for the last year and a half has been that of our data center vertical, working with data center companies, developers across the country. So, living here in Wytheville and learning so much about what the county has been through and what the town is going through, it's mass opportunity and mass change, and I felt it pertinent to at least correlate what I've seen in those 25 years and what I've seen greatly in the last 5 to 10 years, and really speeding up the migration. And there are two points after reading your draft number four that jumped out at me that are not included in draft number four, and those two points are sustainability and agility. And if you don't remember anything else I say, because we've only got two minutes, just remember sustainability and agility, because the next stat that I wanted to share, due to the rapid growth of the industry, is expected to last. We know the AI movement will last for a while. We don't know how long it's going to last. A lot of folks expect this to be, a lot of companies are planning at least five years of this rapid, rapid growth. And again, that's just me and the industry, I'm not speaking on behalf of my current company in any capacity. It's just, this is just my comments. But over those five years, when the market does reach maturity, when AI reaches maturity, what the research shows is that the market will be left with at least 50 to 60% data center. That that is the expectation. So, consider this everything the way business is done to now. What the makeup of our MUSH market, your muni's, your utilities, your schools, the hospitals, they'll now be a category, very sizable category for data centers. So, back to sustainability. I know we don't have a sustainability group or effort or sustainability plan in Wythe County. Sustainability is basically our ability to, you know, weather any storm, to continue to grow, you know, to continue to make sure everybody has enough and is able to continue to grow economically, so doing this responsibly, I think we deserve to have each community deserves to have a sustainability plan. That's Wytheville, that's Fort Chiswell, that's Rural Retreat. I believe what we're missing there is a sustainability policy. Okay, thank you.” Mike Forrest – “I have only a couple comments. First and foremost, I am for planning, for zoning. I believe it builds a path that makes it better, easier to follow for the planning committee for industries coming to town. Secondly, there's 95 counties in the state. 8 of them, including Wythe County, do not have county-wide zoning. There's something got to be wrong if 92% of the counties have zoning and it's working for them. We need to have it too. That's all I have. Thank you.” Sarah Bates – “Hi, I’m Sarah Bates, and thank you for the opportunity to come and express my feelings. I want to start out by saying I feel frustrated and angry. I don't feel like you, as the Planning Commission, is really listening to those of us that have been most invested in coming to these meetings. One of the people I'm here with tonight lives on property where they've clearly expressed to you, they object to the designation for being ag land changed to being commercial. It's incredibly frustrating for them that they October 26, 2026 Public Hearing Unapproved Minutes overheard a member of the Board of Supervisors saying, ‘Well, it's money and power that brought that change.’ When we've been so clear, coming over and over, listening, watching you guys look parcel by parcel, but you aren't listening to those of us that feel like sustainability is broader than what you were just told. To me, sustainability is the ecology, the environment here, and this direction is already just adding to the damage we're all experiencing on Earth right now. I think it's time that everyone wake up and realize climate change is real, and we shouldn't be doing things to further it. We should be doing things to start to work to heal things, and I think it really matters in an agricultural county. So I'm angry, I'm frustrated, I'm trying to be calm and clear about it, but I don't feel like we are being heard as the regular people. If big money is running this, then you got it wrong in my mind. Thank you.” Donna Nichter – “Hi, Donna Nichter. I don't have a lot new to say. I think you've heard me say it before. I wasn't going to speak tonight, but I'm mad, so I decided to speak. I've been opposing data centers since last announced in December, and when we started Preserve Wythe, it was our understanding that zoning is the biggest way to stop any more from coming to Wythe County. At least at that point, we have public hearings, which are so well attended. The apathy in this county is disturbing. I started fighting for the entire county and then found out that it was actually in my backyard that I need to worry about in Whispering Pines. It was our understanding that agriculture would remain agriculture. I have cows up to my fence. I just have a small yard. It's not the best view in Wythe County, but it's sweet. That's why we bought there. That's why the whole neighborhood bought there. I listened to the conversation back and forth between the joint meetings, and there was a lot of ideas. You know, should we do this? Should we do that? Should we do this? But it was decided that the property right behind my fence, where the cows come up to, I talk to them, I sing to them, they're cool. All right. In front of my face on that big screen, it was changed from green to blue, right up to my fence. I'd like to know what that's going to do to my property values. I have no idea what they're planning on doing there. Maybe nothing, but I don't think it's going to help my property value. I was incensed when that was changed in front of my face. I've had so many conversations, so many emails. It felt like a gut punch. I would like to know how many of you, when you're looking at that map, actually know the areas that you're looking at, or do you just see colors? Seems to me that it comes down to quote ‘important families’, but we're all important, money, landowners, and cronies. That's a familiar history. That's all I got to say.” Hannah Ainsworth – “Hello, Hannah Ainsworth. I didn't plan on speaking tonight, so I'll keep it short. To be honest, I didn't really ever think about zoning that much until December 2025, which, when of course, was when the first data center was announced coming to our county, and as I shared, as I spoke at one of the county board meetings after that announcement, my immediate concern with that news was the recognition that inviting one in, rolling out the red carpet for one, whether that be in an industrial park or not, was rolling out the red carpet for across this county. We've seen it time and time again. We've seen it in Northern Virginia, where these data centers proliferate, and I'm October 26, 2026 Public Hearing Unapproved Minutes proud of our county. I love our county. My family has roots to this county for 200 some years. I live here and stay here because I love the region that we're in, and I think we need to preserve this region. I think you know, as zoning is a tool. I think it's important, and I support the use of zoning to protect this county and to give the public an opportunity to speak and give input on what should and should not come to our area. I won't go into a lot of the data center information. I've talked at a couple of the county board meetings. A lot of others have spoken about the harms and concerns there. I would encourage anyone who hasn't watched some of those to go back and watch them. And yeah, so that's it. I'm very supportive of any tool that this county has to keep data centers out. Thank you.” Rusty Jones – “I’m Rusty Jones. I live on the edge of the county. We're on the edge of the town, just adjacent to the county on Reed Creek. I have a 60-acre farm that we live on. I want to just say straight up front, I support what you are doing, I think we need zoning in this county. We've needed it a long time. I appreciate the work of the planning commission. Y'all put a lot of work into this, and I think you kind of gone unthanked for it. And I appreciate all the work y'all done. But I've lived on my farm, well, I've owned it for 20 years, and I'm zoned agriculture in the town because we have zoning. I've got a lot of friends that are farmers. You know, I've done taxes for people over the years and other things, so I know a lot of people in this county, and I know what their fears are of zoning, and what they're afraid of. And I wanted to speak tonight just to alleviate some of their fears. You know, I farm happily inside the town limits of Wytheville, zoned, and it works. You know, I've made a few changes to my property over the years. I've sold off a little bit and gone through some of the zoning processes to do that. Changed some property lines around, and if you give it a chance, I think you'll like it because in the end, I trust my neighbors more than I trust the governor, and more than I trust the president, or Congress, or the House of Representatives, or perhaps even the Board of Supervisors. You know, I mean, a group of my neighbors I believe I can come talk with about what we think would be the best things for Wythe County, and I think as neighbors we all listen to each other. So, it's been a long time coming. And all I wanted to say was, I thank the people that have brought us to this point, and I hope the people that need to … now? I've got a sister-in-law, and her granddaughter lives in South Boston. They have a data center right now, right now, their fish are dying in the river because there's not enough October 26, 2026 Public Hearing Unapproved Minutes

Page 1 of 24 BYLAWS OF THE BOTETOURT COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION January 12, 2026 I. OBJECTIVES The objectives of the Planning Commission shall be as established by § 15.2-2200 of the Code of Virginia, in force on the date hereof, and may from time to time be lawfully amended. II. MEMBERS The Planning Commission shall consist of five voting members, appointed by the Board of Supervisors. There shall be one voting member from each of the County's five magisterial districts. Each shall be qualified by knowledge and experience to make decisions on questions of community growth and development. At least three of the voting members shall be owners of real property in the county. The Board of Supervisors may require each member of the commission to take an oath of office. There shall be one ex officio, non-voting member of the Commission, who shall be a member of and appointed by the Board of Supervisors. Terms shall be for four years. Vacancies shall be filled by appointment for the unexpired term only. Members may be removed for malfeasance in office. The Board of Supervisors may provide for compensation to commission members for their services, reimbursement for actual expenses incurred, or both. III. CHAIRPERSON AND VICE-CHAIRPERSON A Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson of the Commission shall be elected by the Commission annually from the voting members. The Chairperson of the Planning Commission shall preside at all meetings of the Commission. In the event of the absence or disability of the Chairperson, the ViceChairperson shall preside. In the event of the absence or disability of both the Chairperson and ViceChairperson, the remaining members of the Commission shall elect by a majority vote a temporary Chairperson who shall preside at the meeting for which they are elected. The Chairperson of the Planning Commission shall perform such other duties as are designated Page 2 of 24 by statute or by the bylaws of this Commission. In event of the absence or disability of the Chairperson, the Vice-Chairperson shall, to the extent permitted by statute, perform the duties of the Chairperson. IV. SECRETARY The County's Zoning Administrator shall serve as Secretary of the Planning Commission. The Secretary shall keep the minutes, books and records of the Commission. V. DUTIES The duties of the Planning Commission shall be as established by law, or as lawfully delegated by the Board of Supervisors. VI. QUORUM A majority of the voting members of the Planning Commission shall constitute a quorum. Except when otherwise required by statute, or duly adopted rule of procedure, the vote of a majority of those present shall prevail. VII. AGENDA The Secretary shall prepare and make available to each member of the Commission a detailed agenda at least one (1) day prior to each regular meeting of the Commission. The agenda may be departed from with the consent of the Chairperson or by a majority vote of the members present. It shall be the responsibility of each member to notify the Secretary of any matter which such member wishes included on the agenda. Any matter not disposed of at a meeting shall be included on the agenda of the next regular meeting. For any special meeting, the business to be discussed shall be stated in the call for such meeting. No other business shall be discussed or acted upon over the objection of any member present. VIII. HEARINGS Any advertised public hearing shall be considered a special order of business at the time set for such hearing and shall supplant any matter on the agenda except the approval of the minutes. When persons desire to be heard upon matters not on the agenda, the consent of the Chairperson Page 3 of 24 or a majority of the Members present shall be required. At a hearing, and at the discretion of the Chairperson, no person shall be allowed to speak more than three (3) minutes nor more than once upon any particular question. Cumulative or repetitive testimony shall not be permitted on any matter, and persons of the same position as a previous speaker shall state their names and the position with which they agree. Agenda items and discussion topics will be presented by staff, at the discretion of the chair. For matters in which a third party is requesting an action by the Planning Commission, the applicant shall normally be granted fifteen (15) minutes to present their request, which will be followed by hearing comments from interested persons. The Chairperson may, in his/her discretion, deviate from this rule. When all public testimony has concluded, the Planning Commission shall consider and discuss the matter without interruption from the audience. IX. RULES OF ORDER The deliberations of the Planning Commission, unless otherwise provided by statute or these bylaws, shall be governed by "A Handbook of Parliamentary Procedure" (Publication 305-772, Virginia Cooperative Extension Service), with the exception that the Chairperson may make a motion and will vote on any issue, and no second is required on motions. If the foregoing is inapplicable, then Robert's Rules of Order, for small boards, shall govern. Appeal may be taken by any member from a ruling of the Chair. A majority vote of those members present shall determine any appeal. Any motion to close debate shall require approval by two-thirds (2/3) vote of those members present. X. REGULAR MEETINGS The regular meetings of the Planning Commission shall be held on the second Mondayof each month, beginning at 6:00 p.m. in the Botetourt County Administration Center at 57 South Center Drive, Daleville, Virginia, provided, that when the second Monday of any month falls upon a legal holiday such regular meeting in such month shall be held on the next following business day; and provided further, that the Planning Commission may, by resolution at any meeting, Page 4 of 24 provide that the next following regular meeting shall be held at a different time or place, and it shall then be the duty of the Secretary to give timely notice thereof to all members and to inform the news media. XI. SPECIAL MEETINGS Special meetings of the Commission may be convened as required by §15.2-2214. Meetings. of the Code of Virginia. XII. ELECTRONIC MEETINGS Individual members of the Commission may participate in meetings electronically under the provisions of § 2.2-3708.3(B) of the Code of Virginia and pursuant to this Policy. On or before the day of a meeting, a member of the Commission must notify the Chair that: a. Such member is unable to attend the meeting due to a temporary or permanent disability or other medical condition that prevents the member's physical attendance; or b. A medical condition of a member of the member of the Commission’s family requires the Commission member to provide care that prevents the member’s physical attendance, or the Commission member is a caregiver who must provide care for a person with a disability at the time of the meeting, and is therefore unable to attend; or c. The member’s principal residence is more than 60 miles from the published meeting location; or d. Such member is unable to attend the meeting due to a personal matter and identifies with specificity the nature of the personal matter. Participation by a member pursuant to this subdivision is limited each calendar year to two meetings. In order for a member to participate electronically, a quorum of the Commission must be assembled at a single physical location. If the person is a disabled person or a caregiver for a disabled person as defined in § 51.5-40.1 of the Code of Virginia who is unable to attend under subsection a. or b. above, they shall be counted toward the physically assembled quorum, notwithstanding their actual remote participation. The Secretary shall record in the minutes the remote location from which the member participated and the reason why the electronic participation was authorized. Page 5 of 24 The Commission may meet by electronic communication means without a quorum physically assembled at one location when the Governor or the locality has declared a state of emergency, provided that (i) the catastrophic nature of the declared emergency makes it impracticable or unsafe to assemble a quorum in a single location and (ii) the purpose of the meeting is to address the emergency or to provide for continuity of operations of the Commission or its lawful purposes, duties, and responsibilities. In such circumstance, the Commission shall: a. Give public notice using the best available method given the nature of the emergency, which notice shall be given contemporaneously with the notice provided to members of the public body conducting the meeting; b. Make arrangements for public access to such meeting through electronic means; c. Provide a public comment period at such times as comments are normally received in Commission meetings; and d. Otherwise comply with the provisions of this section. The nature of the emergency, the fact that the meeting was held by electronic communication means, and the type of electronic communication means by which the meeting was held shall be stated in the minutes. Page 9 of 24 Addendum to Envision 2045 Solar Energy Systems and Battery Energy Storage Facilities Policies Careful consideration of the location and potential impacts of an alternative energy facility is an essential component of the development process. The design and siting of these facilities should consider the preservation of forested areas, steep slopes, movement of wildlife, and the potential density or concentration of these facilities in one area of a locality, which may impact on the character of an area or limit future growth and development options for available land. These renewable energy uses should continue to be regulated consistently with the County’s values and rural character, along with best practices. 1. When considering applications for minor- and utility-scale solar energy facilities pursuant to Code of Virginia § 15.2-2241.2, 15.2-2288.7, and 15.2-2288.8, the County should consider the following factors, considerations, and potential impacts associated with the proposed facility and its compatibility with the Comprehensive Plan, surrounding development, and public health, safety, and welfare. a. Minor- and utility-scale solar facilities, if built, are preferred to be located on: i. Rooftops and/or over parking lots, particularly when sited on or and adjacent to industrial, commercial, and civic buildings; ii. Brownfields and previously developed sites; iii. Land adjacent to industrial zones; iv. Areas with minimal environmental sensitivity, with terrain that is either flat or gently sloped; and v. Land that is adequately distanced from residential areas (at least 1 mile). b. Minor- and utility-scale solar facilities, if built, are preferred not to be located on: i. Parcels with significant topographical challenges; ii. Areas with sensitive wildlife habitats; iii. Locations near existing solar facilities; iv. High traffic corridors and scenic areas; and v. Prime agricultural farmland. c. Active components (i.e., solar panels, substations, inverters, etc.) or developed features (i.e., fences, gates, maintenance and operations buildings, etc.) of utilityscaled solar facilities should not be located in close proximity to residences or Addendum | Utility-Scale Solar Energy and Battery Energy Storage Facility Policies Page 10 of 24 A-1 historic, cultural, recreational, and environmentally sensitive areas and resources to result in negative impacts to their use, value, or importance individually or to the County. Appropriate buffers and screening should be incorporated to address project proximity to residences, historic and cultural resources. d. Utility-scale solar energy facilities, including fencing and support equipment, should be significantly and sufficiently screened from the view of adjacent properties and rights-of-way by a buffer that consists of natural vegetation and landforms and/or be landscaped with plant materials consisting of an evergreen and deciduous mix. Landscaping materials should be native to the region and exclude the use of invasive species. e. Utility-scale solar energy facilities should incorporate wildlife corridors and wildlife-friendly design measures, where practicable, in accordance with guidance from the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources (DWR), the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR), and other applicable agencies or recognized standards. Such measures may include, but are not limited to, wildlife passages, modified fencing design, habitat connectivity, and protection of sensitive environmental features, consistent with the DWR’s Solar Energy Facility Guidance and similar guidance documents. f. Utility-scale solar energy facilities should include pollinator-smart designated areas to support native species, enhance biodiversity, reduce erosion, and help maintain the County's rural and agricultural character. At least 10% of the project area should be dedicated to pollinator-friendly habitats established and managed using native vegetation and recognized best practices. g. Utility-scale solar energy facilities should generally be in close proximity to transmission line corridors (1 mile or less, measured from the farthest parcel boundary) to reduce the need for significant new infrastructure. Any generation lead lines should be located underground or buffered to block visibility from roadways. h. To ensure the protection of agricultural and forested lands and the rural character of the County, utility-scale solar facilities should be no closer than 1 mile to another facility; individual utility-scale solar facilities should have a total active developed area, including fenced area and area comprising buffers, of less than 500 acres (0.78 square miles); and the total acreage of land in the County utilized for utilityscale solar facilities should be no more than 5,000 acres (7.8 square miles or 1.4% of the total County’s area). i. Utility-scale solar energy facilities should be encouraged to allow for the concurrent use of compatible agricultural, commercial, industrial, or passive recreational uses within project sites. Project developers are also encouraged to preserve undeveloped portions of project properties through conservation easements or similar land conservation mechanisms that limit future development of the property. j. Utility-scale solar energy facilities should provide maximum economic benefits to the County as demonstrated by thorough economic analysis. When considering utility-scale solar applications that do not include battery energy storage systems as part of the original application, the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors should evaluate whether the solar project site can safely accommodate a future onsite battery energy storage system, including the availability of adequate: a. Area; b. Primary access; c. Emergency access; d. Infrastructure capacity; e. Proximity to water supply and fire suppression/detection equipment; and f. Physical separation from surrounding properties (particularly residential uses, historic properties, and scenic byways). Staff reports prepared during the solar application review process and any conditions attached to the special exception permit for the utility-scale solar application should adequately address the potential for battery energy storage on the project site in the future to best protect sensitive surrounding uses. 3. There is a preference for locally generated power to be utilized locally to benefit industrial and other development. Applications for solar facilities and battery energy storage facilities should demonstrate through information and materials how generated electricity will be utilized locally. 4. There is a preference for projects that significantly mitigate or preserve portions of the County in order to protect soils and other natural resources. The following may be considered: a. There was none. BUCKINGHAM COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OCTOBER 13, 2026 - 416- Re: Presentations: Resolution in Memoriam for the family of Henry Wood Chambers: Next is presentations. The first one on the list is the family of Mr. Henry Wood. Would the family of Mr. Wood to come? Mr. Henry Wood. Supervisor Palmore presented the Resolution to the family. RESOLUTION IN MEMORIAM REGARDING THE LIFE AND SERVICE OF HENRY EDWARD WOOD, JR. WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. passed from this life on July 3, 2026 at the age of 78 years old; WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. was born May 9, 1948 to Henry Wood Sr. and Nancy Wood; WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. leaves behind to honor his memory his loving wife of almost 60 years, Dixie Connaster Wood, three children, Eddie (Courtney), Christy Pribble (Marty), and Lacy (Rebecca); seven grandchildren, Jacob Pribble, Madison Pribble, Rose Wood, Reagan Wod, Caleb Wood, Nate Wood and Finley Wood; WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. was a founding member of the Buckingham County Volunteer Rescue Squad, a member of the Arvonia Volunteer Fire Department, a 50 year member of the Stonewall Masonic Lodge #200, served as Deacon in several churches with the last fifteen years being with First Baptist Church of Dillwyn; WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr., even as a young boy, felt he was born to be a farmer and help feed the world. He was a career farmer. He was elected by his peers on a national level to be the Pork All American hog farmer in 1974 and served more than a decade on the Board of Directors for the Virginia Farm Bureau. He ran a prosperous cattle farm in his last 30 years. WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. loved farming, but his truest love was his family. He loved watching his children and grandchildren play sports and was at every game no matter where it was. He taught the boys to hunt and trap and most importantly to be good sportsmen. WHEREAS, Henry Edward Wood, Jr. was well respected and loved by all who knew him. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the members of the Buckingham County Board of Supervisors do hereby recognize and express our deepest appreciation to Henry Edward Wood, Jr. for his many years of dedicated service to Buckingham County. We express our deepest condolences to his family and friends. Palmore: I'd just like to say Henry was a good friend of mine. I served on the deacon board at First Baptist with him. He was just a good man. He did a lot behind the scenes that nobody had any idea that he did. He did so much to help people in the community, and I miss him very much. BUCKINGHAM COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OCTOBER 13, 2026 - 417 - Re: Presentations: Cody Smith and Charlotte Drake, Peter Francisco Soil and Water Conservation District Annual Update Chambers: Next, Cody Smith and Charlotte Drake. Cody Smith: Good evening. I'm Cody Smith with Peter Francisco. I'm representing them tonight. Charlotte Drake is our Education Coordinator. She's the one passing out our annual reports. We do not have a presentation this year. We kind of just try to make this as quick and painless as possible. But anyways, good evening. Thank you for allowing us the time to provide an update on our activities over the past year, we continue to be here as a resource for you and Board members, county staff, and the community members. And you are welcome to call on any of us, directors or staff. We have two cost share programs, and they are broken up into two different areas: agricultural and residential. The Virginia Agricultural Cost Share Program, also known as VAX, is provided by the Virginia Park Department of Conservation and Recreation. As of right now, there are a total of 15 agricultural projects between last year and this year's funding that are under contract, construction as of today in both Buckingham and Cumberland. Those projects total the amount of funding is approximately $878,000. We expect that number to be much higher next month, but we moved our meeting up to this month this year. Applications are taken continuously. We encourage landowners, producers to reach out to us at any time to discuss potential product projects. Secondly, our residential program it offers financial assistance to homeowners on the septic system maintenance. We manage three different grants. One is federally funded through the TMDL 319 grant for the Slate River Watershed, only located in Buckingham County. The second one is a local grant, which covers the remaining portion of Buckingham. Lastly, one is managed through the National Foundation of Wildlife, NIFWIF. That's our acronym for it, and covers Cumberland only. The Slate River TMDL grant has reimbursed Buckingham owners a total of $8,205 since last year. For those outside the Slate River only in Buckingham, the local grant has reimbursed Buckingham a total of $15,992.50. This is a reimbursement program, and reimbursements can take up to 45 days, depending on Board approval and the amount of time it takes for us to receive necessary forms back. For more information about the program, you can either contact me or Charlie or visit our website. Kelly and the office continue to provide plan review services for the Erosion Sediment Control Program for the county in the 2026 calendar year. Working with Lyn and Nicci, Kelly reviewed three plans and consulted on a few site visits as needed. Lastly, on the agricultural side, I guess you could say, we maintain 17 dams that are strictly just in Buckingham County. They are flood prevention sediment control dams. As of for the year, both all dams have been mown twice. We will be performing our annual inspections with on specific dams within the next few months, and all 17 of our dams now have satellite remote monitoring devices, so that we can tell what levels are at all times. We also do educational programs, but I will let Charlie explain those in more detail. Thank you. BUCKINGHAM COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OCTOBER 13, 2026 - 418 - Charlotte Drake: In addition to conservation planning and cost share assistance, we offer educational programming for youth and adults. Upon school and/or teachers' requests, we provide conservation education programs to complement SOL requirements. As the Education Coordinator, I welcome teachers to contact me to plan a classroom session, a field day, or an after-school program. For our college scholarships, we offer annual college scholarships to students in Buckingham and Cumberland. Applicants must be a full-time student who is currently enrolled in or who has applied to a college freshman level or undergraduate level curriculum. The district begins advertising the scholarship applications in January, and applications are due back to the district in March. Our recipient for the 2026 scholarship was Emma Ranson of Buckingham, and she is now attending Virginia Tech. For our camps, we offer scholarships for students to attend Youth Conservation Camp and Camp Woods and Wildlife, formerly known as Forestry Camp, as well as support these camps through attendance as camp counselors and education programming. For the Envirothon competition, the district supports local high school students to participate in the Envirothon competition, which is a natural resources competition where high school students are tested on the topics of soils, forestry, aquatics, wildlife, and a current specific environmental issue, and they also prepare an oral presentation in which they solve a real life environmental problem. The requirements for a team are a minimum of five high school students and one adult advisor and/or chaperone. We continue to recruit teachers and coaches and interested students for the team. For our poster contest, the district coordinates with the schools and art teachers to allow students the opportunity to enter a conservation poster contest put on by the VASWCD. This year's theme was "Soil, Where It All Begins", but we are going to be moving our poster contest timeframe from the fall to the spnng. That sums up our activities. We thank you for allowing us time on your agenda tonight. The district appreciates the working relationship that we have with the county. If you have any questions, we'll be glad to answer them. Chambers: Does any Board member have any questions for them? If not, we thank you for coming and making a presentation. Re: Public Comments Chambers: Moving on to Public Comments. Lann: We have five tonight. Starting with Bob Reck, District 1, and Amy Lawhorne will be next. Bob Reck, District 1: Bob Reck, District l, Cartersville Road. I'm here to thank Jamie Shumaker for the help that he has given us. We have at the present time Bright Speed as our phone service and our internet service. It seems that it's every other week we're without service. In September we went for five days without phone service. Last week we went without internet and phone service, so it got to the point BUCKINGHAM COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OCTOBER 13, 2026 -419- where I said, "Okay, I don't want to have to do this to disturb this person", but I made one phone call to Jamie Shumaker. Now remember how many days have gone by. That night I got a phone call from Bright Speed, the man explaining to me that there was a problem and that we'll have service right away. We got service. I can tell you, standing here now, ifl did not make that call to Jamie Shumaker, and he took that situation and ran with it, I'd still probably be without service. So I'm here publicly to thank him. Often times, we always want to make sure that we, you know, have everything done and back and forth. Today, the young lady came into our driveway and striped our driveway so that we'll get Firefly coming in. So can't wait for it for the internet. So we're on the go. So the reason I had to call Jamie was my wife, who is 85 years old, is on the computer, and when you don't have internet, you have nothing, and her iPad wasn't working, and so I had to listen. She goes, "I can't believe this." So I said one call, and Jamie took care of the whole situation. So we thank him, and we thank the Board. Chambers: Thank you, sir. Lann: Amy Lawhorne, District 2, and Kenda Hanuman will be next. Amy Lawhorne, District 2: Good evening, members of the Board. I'm Amy Lawhorne, District 2. I know the Main Street Traffic Calming Study is on tonight's agenda, and I wanted to express my sincere appreciation to this Board, county staff, the Town of Dillwyn, VDOT, and everybody who has helped move this initiative forward. As we've learned, VDOT's Traffic Calming process is extensive, with multiple steps, requirements, and approvals along the way. It's certainly not a simple undertaking, but I believe we've made tremendous progress through collaboration, communication, and a shared commitment to improving safety. I'm encouraged by the momentum we've built, and I hope that we can continue moving forward without any unnecessary delays. I also want to recognize the Buckingham County Sheriffs Office for its continued partnership, including the digital speed signs on Main Street when resources allow, and assisting traffic during community events such as the recent high school homecoming parade. I recognize that our deputies cannot be everywhere at once, and their efforts are greatly appreciated. As I've shared previously, there are more than 14 children currently liv~ng on Main Street, along with family and residents who regularly walk our neighborhood. But this is more than about Main Street, and even more than about the Town of Dillwyn. This corridor serves people throughout Buckingham County and beyond, whether they're traveling to school, church, local businesses, or just passing through. And while I live within the town limits, I'm also a Buckingham County resident, and I believe that we share the responsibility to consider the safety of everybody who lives, works, and travels through our communities, regardless of municipal boundaries. I understand the importance of being responsible stewards of taxpayer dollars. That's precisely why completing the engineering study is very important. It allows us to gather objective information and determine what, if anything, is warranted, rather than making decisions based on assumptions, I'm grateful for the progress that we've made, and I'm hopeful that we can maintain the positive momentum and continue working BUCKINGHAM COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OCTOBER 13, 2026 · 420 - together toward a safer Main Street for everybody. So, thank you for your time and your service and your consideration. Chambers: Thank you, ma'am. Who's next? Lann: Kenda Hanuman, District 5, and George Goodwin will be next. Kenda Hanuman. District 5: Good evening, Kenda Hanuman, District 5. Good night to be grateful, huh? You're getting a lot of praise here, and I think you deserve it. You've definitely listened to your constituents, and seems like things are working out. I think people were pretty happy after the Planning Commission meeting in which that amendment was thrown out. I guess is what happened to it. So I hope you continue to do that good work, and want to remind everybody to vote. Be an October voter, don't wait until November. There's no telling what's going to happen between now and then. So thank you. Chambers: Thank you, Ma'am. Lann: George Goodwin, District 6, and David Ball will be next. George Goodwin, District 6: George Goodwin, District 6. Scottsville. I want to also be one to say thank you, every one of you, for helping us and listening to the public and letting us have the voice to defeat the prioritized electric lines as they were. That was very meaningful and very much appreciated. I also want to speak about traffic calming in Dillwyn, particularly. I heard that and I thought about it, and if one person, not even an old person, because breaking a hip, an old person, you're on a clock going down real quick. But just say a child and get a broken hip and a concussion. That family's going to spend over $3,000 just for that medical event alone. Please support that and put the money that's needed to support calming the traffic. Again, thank you guys very much for listening to us. Support Agritourism. That's the name of the game. Chambers: Thank you, sir. Lann: David Ball, District 2. That'll be it. David Ball, District 2: Good evening, David Ball, District 2, and you're gonna have to accept that my voice is a little bit off, and I'm on Main Street. I know events are coming up. Big one for the Town of Dillwyn is gonna be Halloween, which is gonna be the last Saturday of the year, and that's gonna be a lot of people coming down Main Street. It's going to be a very celebrated time, like it has been in the last several years. But you know, … Thank you. Anything else, Mr. Carter? Carter: No, sir. Re: Zoning Matters: Request for Zoning Map Amendment Edmondston: I'll be really quick, Mr. Chairman. I just have this memo for you all. Some information from the last Planning … the Board of Supervisors consider the Zoning Administrator accept an application for a Zoning Map Amendment to change the zoning designation of property owned by Leon Lapp, Applicants Andrew and Amanda Powell, from A-1 Agricultural to B-1 … After consideration and discussion, the Planning Commission determined that a Zoning Map Amendment from A-1 to B-1 would be more appropriate for the property and the proposed use. Planning Commission unanimously recommended that the Board … pleasure of the Board for me, as Zoning Administrator, to accept this application for a Zoning Map Amendment. Chambers: What's the pleasure of the Board? Palmore: I have a question. Is that the shed place, the shed building place? … by the Board of Supervisors for the Zoning Administrator accept the application for Zoning Map Amendment from Mr. and Mrs. Powell. Re: Finance: Consider contract for auditing services for FY2026 with Robinson, Farmer, Cox Assoc. Carter

title: November 5, 2026, City Council Packet
text: CITY OF BUENA VISTA COUNCIL AGENDA REGULAR MEETING NOVEMBER 5, 2026 | 6:00 PM Council Chambers – 2039 Sycamore Avenue ADG #1: CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE, & PRAYER ADG #2: APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA ADG #3: APPROVAL OF MINUTES FROM THE OCTOBER 15, 2026 REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING ADG #4: RECOGNITION/COMMUNICATION FROM VISITORS Citizens who desire to speak to council regarding items NOT listed on the agenda will be recognized at this time. Please limit your statement to three (3) minutes. ADG #5: REPORTS: 1. Mayor 2. City Manager – Managerial Activities Update 3. City Attorney 4. Council Committees/Members 5. Department Heads 6. Invited Community Organizations ADG #6: PRESENTATIONS TO CITY COUNCIL & THE PUBLIC None ADG #7: CONSIDER APPOINTMENTS TO BOARDS, COMMISSIONS, AND COMMITTEES Modiﬁcation of Shenandoah Valley Partnership & Rockbridge Area Tourism Board Appointments OLD BUSINESS NONE NEW BUSINESS NB #1: CONSIDERATION OF AN APPROPRIATION RESOLUTION NB #2: CONSIDERATION OF AMENDED ROADS OF HONOR MOU NB #3: CONSIDERATION OF RESOLUTIONS OF SUPPORT FOR CITY VDOT APPLICATIONS 1 ADJOURNMENT UPCOMING MEETINGS • November 10 | 7:00 PM – Planning Commission • November 11 | 6:00 PM – GMP-OS Committee • November 16 | 6:00 PM – Cemetery Committee • November 17 | 6:00 PM – Citizens Advisory Committee • November 19 | 6:00 PM – City Council UPCOMING EVENTS • Every Monday | 6:30 PM – Line Dancing @ The American Legion • Every Friday | 3:00 PM – Farmers Market @ Magnolia Square • Every Friday | 6:00 PM – Friday Events @ Straws • November 18 | 7:00 PM – Book Club @ Leaf & Lore 2 ADG #3 Draft CITY OF BUENA VISTA CITY COUNCIL REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING October 15, 2026 | 6:00 PM Council Chambers – 2039 Sycamore Avenue The Buena Vista City Council met for a Regular Council Meeting on Thursday, October 15, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. Members Present: Vice-Mayor Danny Staton Amy Gilliam Michelle Poluikis William Kerr Stephanie Noel-Branch Ronald Cash Members Absent: Mayor Jesse Lineberry ADG #1: CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE, & PRAYER Vice-Mayor Staton called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. and Councilmember Kerr delivered the opening prayer. ADG #2: APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA Councilmember Kerr moved to approve the agenda, Councilmember Gilliam seconded, and the motion carried. ADG #3: APPROVAL OF MINUTES FROM THE OCTOBER 1, 2026, REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING, PUBLIC HEARING, & EXECUTIVE SESSION Councilmember Gilliam moved to approve the minutes, Councilmember Noel-Branch seconded, and the motion carried. ADG #4: RECOGNITION/COMMUNICATION FROM VISITORS – NON-AGENDA ITEMS • Tobler Hughes, 1 University Hill Drive, a new Buena Vista resident and student at SVU, introduced himself and expressed his excitement about becoming involved in the community and participating in local service opportunities. • Avery Brinton, 1 University Hill Drive, shared a proposal for a free community car wash organized through SVU. She distributed copies of the proposal to Council members and explained that she is working with SVU’s Service Council and Student Life staﬀ, April Harris and Carrie Brotherson, to coordinate a possible event in early November at Glen Maury Park. She also hopes to partner with the owner of Holy Cow to support the business. ADG #5: REPORTS: 1. Mayor None. 2. City Manager Community Engagement and Outreach: Ms. Onaitis reported that the City continues to receive citizen inquiries and concerns, primarily related to utility billing, including questions about rates and unusually high bills potentially caused by leaks. She also reminded residents that household trash must be placed in a trash can, as placing loose trash at the curb is a code violation. She reported that Mountain Days was a success, with strong attendance downtown and a particularly successful ﬁrst year for the children’s activity zone. She recognized Council members and staﬀ who assisted with the event and noted that Delegate Terry Austin’s oﬃce had reached out with questions about Magnolia Square and the timber frame pavilion. Additional community engagement eﬀorts included a recent BV Beat recording by Chief Clements highlighting the SHIELD program and regional canine training at Glen Maury Park along with police department press releases on crime prevention. She also encouraged residents to visit the fall-themed photo display at Glen Maury Park. She attended the regional social services ribbon-cutting and the Governor’s Summit on Rural Prosperity, where City and regional representatives participated in discussions and showcased the area. She noted the City’s interest in locating a Virginia Department of Health oﬃce near the social services facility to improve access to health and human services. Staﬀ and Process Improvements: Ms. Onaitis reported holding individual meetings with department leadership and conducting the ﬁfth executive team meeting. These meetings take place during weeks when Council does not meet and provide an opportunity for staﬀ to review upcoming agendas and discuss departmental activities. The City continues working to standardize ﬁnance and HR forms to improve consistency, reduce confusion, and support compliance with FOIA and public records retention requirements. A citywide safety training was also completed, with additional training through the Virginia Risk Sharing Association (VRSA) anticipated in January, covering topics such as workers’ compensation, FMLA, and reporting responsibilities. Regarding the RDA ﬁnancial software, IT has met with department heads and constitutional oﬃces to identify system issues and user needs. Staﬀ are compiling the feedback, which will be used to prepare a formal letter to the vendor outlining the City’s concerns. City Operations: She reminded everyone that the 45-day utility billing grace period will end October 24. Residents with questions about their bills were encouraged to contact the City, and accounts must be current by that date to avoid potential fees or service interruptions. The City’s upcoming Pothole Blitz is scheduled for the week of October 26. Residents are encouraged to report potholes by providing the exact location or nearest intersection, with Public Works planning to address as many areas as possible through cold-patch repairs. She also discussed upcoming Halloween activities with Main Street, including the annual trick-ortreating event at the lower campground at Glen Maury Park. She requested Council’s support for temporarily reduced campground rates to encourage campers to participate by handing out candy, providing children with a safe, traditional trick-or-treating experience. She also reported that Hurt & Proﬃtt contractors would be visiting City Hall to assess needed work and provide cost estimates. DEQ Consent Order: Ms. Onaitis reported that she, the Public Works Director, and the City Attorney recently met with the Department of Environmental Quality to discuss concerns with the City’s wastewater consent order. Discussions focused on clarifying the requirements, addressing aggressive deadlines, and working toward a more realistic compliance schedule. She explained that the City is seeking to ensure the consent order reﬂects feasible improvements to the existing wastewater treatment plant through renovation, retroﬁtting, and modernization rather than requiring full replacement of the facility. The City currently has a utility services RFP advertised to secure a ﬁrm that can provide technical assistance with water and wastewater projects, maintenance priorities, funding opportunities, regulatory compliance, and consent order requirements. Economic and Community Development: She reminded Council that the EDA Façade Improvement Program is open, with applications being accepted through November 6. Brownﬁelds applications are expected to open in early spring, with an initial focus on publicly owned properties. She also reported receiving a draft scope of work from Timmons Group for the City’s economic development strategic planning eﬀorts. The project will evaluate approximately 8-10 City-owned properties, considering utility capacity, land use, topography, potential uses, needed improvements, and marketing strategies. The assessment will also consider potential site-readiness funding opportunities and whether certain properties may be better suited for sale to adjacent property owners. She noted that the Police Department continues to increase its public outreach and media presence and recently received the Rising Star Award for the local Triad chapter. Chief Clements also attended the Governor’s First Uniﬁed Readiness Summit, a statewide emergency management exercise. Schools Collaboration: Ms. Onaitis reported that funding analyses related to school needs are ongoing, with several ﬁnancial scenarios expected from the City’s ﬁnancial advisors, Davenport. She reminded Council that the City’s community conversation regarding the proposed additional 1% sales tax is scheduled for October 20 at 6:00 p.m. The meeting will provide information about the referendum, the legally permitted uses of the revenue, and what purchases would be subject to the additional tax. Finance: She advised Council to anticipate an appropriation request at the November meeting related to a delayed vendor invoice for salt purchased in January 2026. Because the purchase occurred during the previous ﬁscal year, but the vendor did not submit the invoice until about 10 months later, an appropriation will be necessary to process a payment. She also provided an update on the expenditure report being developed for Council, which is expected to be presented in November. She cautioned that the report may initially provide budgeted amounts alongside estimated year-to-date expenditures, as staﬀ continue working through the annual audit and outstanding reconciliation items. 3. City Attorney None. 4. Council Committees/Members Mr. Cash thanked Jen and Neil Carpenter for their hard work and contributions to Mountain Days, noting the many hours they devoted to planning and coordinating the events. He shared that he enjoyed the children’s activities and praised the children’s behavior and participation. He noted that the girls won many of the event competitions and highlighted the importance of creating lasting memories for the children. He also discussed opportunities to improve next year’s event, including better signage directing visitors to the children’s area and expanding participation. Mrs. Noel-Branch agreed that the pie-eating contest was a highlight, noting that even one parent joined in and enjoyed the opportunity of making memories. 5. Department Heads/Constitutional Officers/Court Clerks Tom Roberts – Community Development Mr. Roberts provided an update on the Community Garden, explaining that organizers are developing a clearer policy regarding use of the pavilion and conﬁrming that the public is welcome. He also reported on discussions with Austin Rehl of the Rockbridge Creative Institute regarding a proposed U-Pick blackberry operation at Meridian Farmstead on the north end of the City. The project would initially include about two acres, with the potential to expand to eight acres. The City is exploring the Agriculture and Forestry Industries Development (AFID) grant program to help fund the project, with additional details and matching requirements still to be determined. The proposal also includes using the Innovation Accelerator’s commercial kitchen to package harvested blackberries into jams, jellies, and other products. 6. Invited Community Organizations Jen Carpenter – Main Street Buena Vista Mrs. Carpenter began her reported by thanking Council and the community for their support and assistance with Mountain Days, noting that the event was a meaningful and encouraging experience. She announced that MSBV was awarded a $9,000 Downtown Investment Grant through the Governor’s oﬃce. The grant will support a wayﬁnding signage project to improve connections between downtown and other community assets, including Glen Maury Park. She will coordinate with the City Manager regarding the City’s proposed in-kind match. She also reported that 18 people participated in the Buena Vista downtown walking tour during the Governor’s Summit on Rural Prosperity, with positive feedback from attendees. MSBV was also awarded a Virginia State Tourism Homestay grant to promote local lodging options, including Glen Maury Park and short-term rentals. As part of the initiative, Main Street will work with the City to identify registered lodging businesses and help ensure applicable lodging taxes are collected. Mrs. Carpenter also shared that Leaf and Lore received a Virginia State Tourism Grant in collaboration with Virginia Main Street and tourism organizations to develop a Shenandoah Valley book crawl and day-trip itinerary featuring independent bookstores. She announced that the annual Halloween Spooktacular will be held Saturday, October 31, from 4:00 to 6:00 p.m., including the return of the golf cart parade. She also noted that she will work with the City Manager to develop a formal memorandum of understanding between the City and MSBV as part of the organization’s accreditation requirements. An annual impact report will also be prepared and presented to Council. Councilmember Noel-Branch praised Mrs. Carpenter’s work and shared positive feedback received from participants in the Governor’s Summit and walking tour, noting the welcoming atmosphere created by local businesses and the positive impression of Buena Vista. ADG #6: PRESENTATIONS TO CITY COUNCIL & THE PUBLIC Kim Shaw, Rockbridge Area Community Services Ms. Shaw provided an overview of RACS services and recent accomplishments. She reported that RACS served 1,772 individuals during the previous ﬁscal year, including 352 Buena Vista residents, representing approximately 20% of those served. RACS provides services related to mental health, substance use, intellectual and developmental disabilities, and prevention, along with 24-hour emergency services. She reported that RACS has implemented its permanent supportive housing program, with about 15 available placements. One individual has been housed, and additional referrals are pending. She noted a need for additional landlords willing to participate in the program. She also highlighted RACS’ partnership with the local Recovery Court program and the expansion of its intensive outpatient program from one group to three, each serving up to 12 participants. RACS is preparing to expand services at the Eagle’s Nest building in Buena Vista, with renovations underway and a goal of opening by the end of the year. Ms. Shaw also announced the purchase of Maple Hall in Timber Ridge, which is planned for use as a residential substance use treatment facility oﬀering 30, 60-, and 90-day stays. The goal is to provide a full continuum of treatment and recovery services locally, reducing the need for individuals to seek residential treatment outside the area. Ms. BreAnne Rogers shared information about several RACS programs and upcoming events. She encouraged Council to help promote the Magnolia Players’ Christmas performance at the Magnolia Center, scheduled for December 21 and 22 at 1:00 p.m. She also highlighted the monthly veteran breakfast, which typically serves 20-25 veterans and is open to family members, and their ongoing caregiver support group. Ms. Rogers and Ms. Shaw also discussed RACS prevention and peer support eﬀorts, including: • Providing crisis intervention training resources and community prevention information to local law enforcement. • Partnering with the BVPD on their recent cop camp. • Reaching 672 area students through the Catch My Breath vaping prevention curriculum. • Hosting a mental health awareness walk, which drew 63 participants despite rainy weather and included a visit from Oﬃcer Matt Slagle and K-9 Hans. • Scheduling their next annual prevention forum for June 10, 2027. • Expanding peer support services for veterans, individuals experiencing mental health or substance use challenges, and participants in intensive outpatient programs. RACS peer services have assisted about 100 individuals during the year and also provide support at the regional jail, serving approximately 15-20 inmates each week. Cumberland County Public Schools Superintendent, Missy Shores, provided the Board with the following monthly update: School Performance and Student Success As we review our School Performance and Support Framework (SPSF) results for Cumberland Elementary School, Cumberland Middle School, and Cumberland High School, we are reminded that student achievement is a shared responsibility. Each school serves students at a different stage of their educational journey, but our collective goal remains the same: to ensure that every student receives the instruction, support, and opportunities necessary to grow and succeed. Cumberland Elementary School showed tremendous progress. Even with the growth, We went from on track to Distinguished (top 3 in overall SPSF gains), our focus remains on early literacy, foundational mathematics, student engagement, and identifying 5 10132026 BOS 6:00pm Page 5 of 16 individual student needs as early as possible. The work taking place at the elementary level is essential to ensuring that students are prepared for the increasing academic demands they will encounter in the years ahead. Cumberland Middle School crushed it last year. Last year the middle school just avoided being a federally identified school and this year missed by less than 1.5 points, being distinguished. CMS was top 3 in total framework points, top 3 in overall gains, reading growth, math growth, math mastery and science mastery. While we are pleased with these results, we will not stop pushing to continue to get better. Cumberland High School remained distinguished and continues to focus on ensuring students are leaving prepared for what lies beyond high school. Our high school was ranked 2nd in the region in on time graduation. This year we are placing a strong focus on career readiness by upping our efforts to find internships for our students as well as expanding our school-based enterprise. While each school has its own areas of strength and opportunities for improvement, we approach these results as one division. Our administrators and instructional leaders work collaboratively to review data, identify needs, share effective practices, and develop strategies that benefit students across all grade levels. One of Cumberland County Public Schools' greatest strengths is the ability of our administrative team to work together toward a common purpose. We may not always agree on every decision or approach, and healthy professional disagreement is a natural part of effective leadership. However, those conversations happen where they belong—behind closed doors, among the professionals responsible for working through challenges and finding solutions. Once decisions are made, we move forward together. We do not allow individual disagreements to become distractions for our staff, families, students, or community stakeholders. Our responsibility is to provide consistent leadership, maintain confidence in our schools, and keep students at the center of our 6 10132026 BOS 6:00pm Page 6 of 16 decisions. That unity of purpose has contributed to the progress we have made and will continue to be essential to our future success. This is a characteristic that successful organizations strive for. Celebrating Our Schools and Community Our schools have been active in creating meaningful experiences that connect students, staff, families, and the broader Cumberland community. Our annual September 11 remembrance ceremony provided an opportunity to honor those who lost their lives, recognize the courage and sacrifice of first responders and military personnel, and remind our students of the importance of service, unity, and citizenship. These moments help ensure that our students understand the significance of our shared history and the responsibilities that come with being members of a community. At Cumberland Elementary School, the Color Run brought energy, excitement, and school spirit to an event centered on student participation and community involvement. Activities such as this strengthen relationships among students, staff, and families while creating positive memories associated with school. Our Walk for Education highlighted the importance of education as a community-wide commitment. When families, educators, community members, and local leaders come together in support of our students, we reinforce the message that their success matters to all of us. We also appreciate the continued support of those who participated in and contributed to our Foundation Golf Tournament. The Foundation plays an important role in bringing additional resources and opportunities to our schools. Events such as this demonstrate what can be accomplished when community members invest their time, energy, and resources in public education. These activities are more than individual events. They reflect the 7 10132026 BOS 6:00pm Page 7 of 16 strong community spirit that makes Cumberland County special. We are grateful for our local organizations, businesses, volunteers, families, and community leaders who consistently demonstrate a willingness to support our students and schools. Combined, the Walk for Education and the Foundation Golf Tournament raised close to $30,000 for student scholarships and grants for teacher classroom projects. Looking Ahead: Spring Festival We are excited to announce that Cumberland County Public Schools is collaborating with the Cumberland County 4-H Department to host a Spring Festival on April 10. This collaborative event will provide an opportunity to bring our community together while highlighting student participation, educational opportunities, local resources, and the many organizations that contribute to the quality of life in Cumberland County. Our partnership with 4-H is a strong example of how schools and community organizations can work together to create meaningful opportunities for young people. By combining our resources and strengths, we can offer experiences that extend beyond the classroom and help students develop interests, skills, relationships, and a stronger connection to their community. We look forward to sharing more information as plans develop and hope that the community will join us in providing opportunities for showcasing local talent and those who would like may also reach out to be vendors at the event. Budget Planning and Fiscal Responsibility As we begin planning for the upcoming budget cycle, we want to be intentional about our communication and collaboration with the Board of Supervisors. This year, we would like to schedule two budget work sessions with the Board of Supervisors. Our goal is to provide adequate time to review the school division's financial needs, discuss 8 10132026 BOS 6:00pm Page 8 of 16 priorities, examine available resources, and address questions before the formal budget process advances too far. A work session should not just be a presentation of our ask fors, but a look at the process of school finance, which is very different from business or county finance, but also a collaboration of both parties to ensure we are focused on the right things and fulfilling the expectations of our stakeholders. Thank you for your continued support of Cumberland County Public Schools and for your willingness to engage in conversations that will help us plan thoughtfully for the future. We look forward to continuing our work together on behalf of the students, families, and citizens of Cumberland County. b. Cumberland Fire & EMS c. text: GREENSVILLE COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION AGENDA GREENSVILLE COUNTY GOVERNEMENT BUILDING BOARD ROOM Tuesday, November 10, 2026 6:00 p.m. I, CALL TO ORDER I. ROLL CALL Tl. APPROVAL OF AGENDA A. Approval of Minutes — See Attachment — A. 1, October 13, 2026 IV. PUBLIC HEARING A. ZMA-4-2026 Hollyhock Trail Associates LLC — See Attachment —B. V. REGULAR SESSION A. ZMA-4-2026 Hollyhock Trail Associates LLC VI. OTHER MATTERS VU. ADJOURN ATTACHMENT A The Greensville County Planning Commission meeting was held Tuesday, October 13, 2026, 6:00 P.M., in the Board Room of the Greensville County Government Building located at 1781 Greensville County Circle, Emporia, VA 23847. PRESENT Dr. Adrian Chatman, Chairman Jeff Robinson, Vice-Chairman Joe Antorn Jr. Jessica Byrd William Cain Adolph Flowers Nakisha Hardy Chris Thompson ABSENT Sandra Wiggins STAFF PRESENT Linwood E. Pope, Jr. Porscha Wright OTHERS PRESENT Cordaryl Moore Grady A, Palmer Ronnell Pearson Jimmy Wood, Counsel for Verizon Wireless In Re: CALL TO ORDER Chairman Chatman called the meeting of Tuesday, October 13, 2026 to order. Chairman Chatman opened the meeting with prayer. In Re: ROLL CALL Mr. Pope called the roll. Commissioners Antorn, Byrd, and Wiggins were absent. In Re: APPROVAL OF AGENDA Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to approve the agenda as presented. Commissioner Robinson made a motion to approve the agenda, seconded by Commissioner Flowers, with all voting aye, motion carried. In Re: APPROVAL OF THE MINUTES Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to approve the minutes of July 14, 2026. Commissioner Thompson made a motion to approve minutes, seconded by Commissioner Robinson, with all voting aye, motion carried. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to go into public hearing. Commissioner Hardy made a motion to enter into public hearing, seconded by Commissioner Flowers, with all voting aye, motion carried. In Re: PUBLIC HEARING In Re: SP-8-2026 — Audrey Faye Holloway/Verizon Wireless Mr. Pope stated that the applicant, was requesting a Special Use Permit to construct and operate a 250’ self-supporting, monopole telecommunication tower with a 4’ lightning rod together with related wireless antennas and equipment on an approximately 10,000 square foot portion of the referenced 25.00- acre parcel which is zoned A-1, Agricultural. He stated that this property was located at 4367 Grassy Pond Road in the Nottoway District. Mr. Pope stated that after reviewing the Zoning Ordinance and the Comprehensive Plan, Staff feels that the applicants request for a Special Use Permit is consistent with the goals and strategies set forth by the County. Therefore, Staff recommends approval of the applicant’s request subject to the following conditions: APPROVE WITH CONDITIONS 1. A Special Use Permit is granted to Vertical Bridge/Cellco Partnership d/b/a Verizon Wireless, or its assigns for the location of a 250’ self-supporting telecommunications tower, on the property of Audrey Faye Holloway, or her assigns, on Greensville County Tax Map 13-22. 2, The tower shall be erected and maintained in accordance with all local, state, and federal rules, regulations, ordinances, and laws with particular reference to the Federal Communications Commission. 3. The tower shall be erected and maintained in accordance with the regulations set forth in Article 19 of the Greensville County Zoning Ordinance. 4. Should the telecommunications tower subject of this request become completely inoperable for a period of time, meeting or exceeding twenty-four (24) months, such tower shall be dismantled and removed from the site together with its support system and compound area. 3. Should any work take place within VDOT maintained right-of-way, a Land Use Permit from VDOT will be required. 6. Failure to abide by the above conditions may result in the revocation of the Special Use Permit. Mr. Pope stated that the applicant was present and would present their project to the Commission. 2 Mr. Jimmy Wood, counsel for Vertical Bridge-Cellco Partnership, addressed the Commission. He stated that Mr. Pope had outlined the project very well. He stated that the proposed area was underserved but with the construction of this tower, the community would be better served with additional internet access and cellular service to enhance the quality of life. He respectfully requested that the Commission recommend approval of SP-8-2026 to the Greensville County Board of Supervisors. Chairman Chatman invited citizens present, that had comments, to come forward and address the Commission. No one came forward, so she entertained a motion to go into Regular Session. Commissioner Byrd made a motion to go out of Public Hearing and into Regular Session; seconded. by Commissioner Flowers, with all voting Aye, motion was approved. In Re: REGULAR SESSION In Re: SP-8-2026 Audrey Faye Holloway/Verizon Wireless Chairman Chatman asked if there was further discussion. There was none. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion for SP-8-2026. Commissioner Robinson made a motion to recommend approval of SP-8-2026, seconded by Commissioner Thompson. A roll call vote was taken by Mr. Pope. Commissioner Cain YES Commissioner Thompson YES Chairman Chatman YES Commissioner Robinson YES Commissioner Byrd YES Commissioner Hardy YES Commissioner Antorn YES Commissioner Flowers YES With a six (8) YES, zero (0) NO vote, the motion carried to recommend approval of SP-8-2026 Audrey Faye Holloway/Verizon Wireless Special Use Permit. Mr. Pope stated that this recommendation would be presented to the Greensville County Board of Supervisors at their next meeting. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to go into public hearing. Commissioner Flowers made a motion to enter into public hearing, seconded by Commissioner Byrd, with all voting aye, motion carried. In Re: PUBLIC HEARING In Re: SP-9-2026 — Cordary! Moore/Moore Motion LLC Mr. Pope stated that the applicant was requesting a Special Use Permit (SUP) to conduct large special events / horse trail-riding activities on a 103.23-acre tract located at 3650 Taylors Mill Road, Skippers, Virginia, identified as Tax Map Number 46-44. He stated that because the subject property and surrounding properties are zoned A-1 Agricultural, the proposed large special events and horse trail-riding activities require review and approval through the applicable Special Use Permit process. He also stated that the property is served by an existing private well and septic drainfield. The existing well and septic system may continue to serve the property's normal permitted uses, subject to applicable requirements. Due to the increased attendance and sanitation demands associated with large special events, portable restroom facilities and supplemental handwashing stations shall be provided for event attendees in accordance with applicable Virginia Department of Health requirements. Large-event wastewater shall not exceed the permitted capacity of the existing septic system. Being no other public comments, Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to go into regular session. Commissioner Byrd made a motion to go out of public hearing into regular session, seconded by Commissioner Flowers; with all voting aye, motion carried, RE: REGULAR SESSION. In Re: SP-9-2026 — Cordary! Moore/Moore Motion LLC Chairman Chatman asked if there was further discussion. There was none. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion for SP-9-2026. Commissioner Byrd made a motion to recommend approval of SP-9-2026, seconded by Commissioner Cain. A roll call vote was taken by Mr. Pope. Comiunissioner Cain YES Commissioner Thompson YES Chairman Chatman ABSTAIN Commissioner Robinson YES Commissioner Byrd YES Commissioner Hardy YES Commissioner Antorn YES Commissioner Flowers YES With a seven (7) YES, zero (0) NO vote, one (1) abstain, the motion carried to recommend approval of SP-9-2026 Cordary! Moore/Moore Motion LLC. Special Use Permit. Mr. Pope stated that this recommendation would be presented to the Greensville County Board of Supervisors at their next meeting. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to go into Public Hearing. Commissioner Hardy made a motion, seconded by Commissioner Byrd, with all voting aye, motion carried. 4 RE: PUBLIC HEARING In Re: SP-10-2026 — Pear IV, LLC Mr. Pope stated that the applicant Ronnel! Pearson is requesting a Special Use Permit to construct and operate a Funeral Home on approximately 23.19 acres identified as Greensville County Tax Map 21- 23 located in the Belfield Election District, zoned A-1, agricultural and is currently a vacant cutover. The property is served by an existing 8-inch water main and an existing 8-inch sewer force main, providing access to public water and wastewater infrastructure, subject to verification of capacity and applicable utility approvals. Mr. Pope stated that the Zoning Ordinance also recognizes that certain business and other nonresidential uses may be appropriate within the A-1 District when reviewed through the Special Use Permit process. He further stated a funeral home is a service-oriented use that may generate traffic associated with funeral services, visitations, employees, deliveries, and funeral processions. The primary land-use considerations associated with the request include: Vehicular access; Traffic circulation; Parking; Funeral procession staging; Exterior lighting; Noise; Building setbacks; Parking setbacks; Landscaping and screening; Stormwater drainage; Water and wastewater facilities; and Emergency vehicle access. Mr. Pope stated that subject to compliance with the approved site plan and recommended conditions, the proposed use can be designed and operated in a manner that is consistent with the applicable goals and policies of the Greensville2040 Comprehensive Plan and the purposes and intent of the A-1 Agricultural District. Mr. Pearson addressed the commission stating that he has spoken with the adjacent land owners to keep them informed on the project and everyone was in agreeance with the project. He respectfully requested that the Commission recommend approval of SP-10-2026 to the Greensville County Board of Supervisors. Chairman Chatman entertained a motion to go into regular session. Commissioner Flowers made a motion fo go back into Regular Session, seconded by Commissioner Thompson; with all voting Aye, motion carried.
